speechtext:
Mr. JEAN-FltANQOIS POULIOT (Temis-couata): As a private Liberal member of this hon. house I rise to a question of privilege.
On April 28, Colonel the Hon. J. L. Ralston, Minister of National Defence, is reported at page 1968 of Hansard as having spoken as follows:
There are a certain number of professional soldiers, and thank heaven there are, because we did not treat our professional soldiers any too well, at least during the period when I was Minister of National Defence previously. I take my share of responsibility for that. From 1926 to 1930 the army and national defence services were nearly starved, and I make that statement now. It seemed to me that perhaps the most popular indoor sport in those days was cutting amounts off the estimates for national defence, and the hon. member for Temiscouata did his share of advocating that this be done. Now I say to my hon. friend that in spite of all that, the men who were professional soldiers did keep on.
With regard to the two first above quoted sentences, such a confession of incompetence and incapacity has been delayed for a considerable time indeed, but it had to be made in due course and it is duly acknowledged.
The second part of the above quotation is even more absurd than malicious. Who would believe that the then Minister of National Defence did ever substitute for four years or for a minute the advice of the member for Temiscouata for that of all the pompous brass hats that adorn the Department of National Defence?
What are the facts? The hon. Minister of National Defence was elected for the first time to the House of Commons in September, 1926.

speechtext: Order. On a question of privilege the hon. member is of course entitled to refute anything that has been said which he thinks is a breach of the privileges of hon. members, but I would not wish the hon. member to think that he can make an extended argument-

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON IN DEBATE ON APRIL 28
speechtext: I am not making an argument, Mr. Speaker; I am stating facts.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON IN DEBATE ON APRIL 28
speechtext: You certainly are.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON IN DEBATE ON APRIL 28
speechtext: My hon. friend should keep quiet and listen to learn what I am doing now. I am not making an argument; I am stating facts, which is the privilege of an hon. member. I do not contend that any hon. member is supposed to withdraw what he said about another hon. member if he does not use unparliamentary language, but when a statement of fact is made in relation to an hon. member, that member unquestionably has the right to state the relevant facts as he sees them, and that is what I am doing now.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON IN DEBATE ON APRIL 28
speechtext: Make it short.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. POULIOT REFERENCE TO STATEMENT OF MR. RALSTON IN DEBATE ON APRIL 28
speechtext:
Between September 1926 and 1930 there were four sessions of parliament. I have the index of Hansard for each of those sessions, and in those for 1926-27 and 1929 I challenge the minister to find anything that I said1 concerning his department. The only question that I asked him in the session of 1928 was on the estimates and in connection with the establishment of a landing field at Riviere du Loup. The minister answered that he had nothing to do with it. That was all for that year.
With regard to the session of 1930, in order to prepare my speech on Mr. Bennett's amendment to the budget I had asked all the cabinet ministers what they considered their greatest accomplishments, and I assumed personal responsibility for what the Minister of National Defence and his colleagues told me when I included their notes in my speech to boost my party before the general elections of that year.
I have sent the four Hansard indexes of those sessions to the Minister of National Defence, and they are on his desk. I challenge him to prove his erroneous contention that the hon. member for Temiscouata did his share of advocating the most popular indoor sport in those days, cutting amounts off from the estimates for national defence.
Privilege-Mr. Pouliot

With regard to the last sentence of the above quotation, the truth shall never be falsified even by a self-centred miniature navel of the whole world.

PRIVILEGE-MR. ESLING OBJECTION TO REMOVAL OF JAPANESE NATIONALS TO MUNICIPALITY OF KASLO, B.C
speechtext:
On a question of privilege, Mr. Speaker, I would ask to be permitted to make a statement on a matter of immediate and vital importance to my riding. As is well known, there is in progress a movement of Japanese from the British Columbia coast to areas east of the Cascade mountains. According to a Canadian Press report from Vancouver under date of March 10, the chairman of the British Columbia security commission, under whose direction the movement is being carried out, is credited with the statement that Japanese will not be moved to any area until opinion is unanimously in favour of that being done.
Recently officials at Kaslo, a community on Kootenay Lake, invited the chairman to send a contingent of Japanese into that city, and preparations are now under way for the housing of women, children and aged Japanese men. On the other hand I have a protest signed by 112 Kaslo citizens protesting vigorously against the bringing in of the Japanese. In last year's census Kaslo was recorded as having a population of 463. In the opinion of the dominion statistician 30 to 40 per cent is a conservative estimate of the proportion of children in a municipal census. It may be accepted therefore that the 112 who protested are a representative proportion of the adult community. It is in order that we might avoid factional feelings, ill will and perhaps bitterness that I have been requested by those who protest to ask the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) to interest themselves in this matter, in the light of the statement by the chairman that these Japanese would not be placed in any community without unanimous approval.
This matter is of real importance not only in its relation to Kaslo but in its relation to other communities. Perhaps the difficulty has arisen because of the original statement that the northern boundary of the prohibited area in West Kootenay was to be the fiftieth parallel. In that event Kaslo would have been included in the prohibited area. But for some reason perhaps best known to the Minister of Justice that area was changed; thus we have the difficulty to which I direct the attention of the government.

maintopic: PRIVILEGE-MR. ESLING OBJECTION TO REMOVAL OF JAPANESE NATIONALS TO MUNICIPALITY OF KASLO, B.C
speechtext:
It is difficult to get unanimous agreement to put the Japanese anywhere. I believe in almost all cases where we have
(Mr. J. A. MacKinnon.]

Privilege-Mr. Esling
been, able to move them there has been a considerable body of opinion against their being moved to particular localities. In view of the situation at the coast I think in the national interest too much notice should not be taken of that.
A request came from the board of trade of the district to which the hon. member has referred, and there was a further request from the mayor of that community. I believe it would be fair to say that Kaslo is what might be known as a ghost town. A number of ghost towns in that area sent in requests- four of them, to be exact-that the Japanese be removed to those communities. The commission sent in an inspector, and after investigation contracts were let for the repair of houses in which Japanese women and children cculd be placed. It is estimated that we can put about 5,000 persons in those particular communities.
I have been out there and looked over the ground, and it does make it very difficult for those charged with the responsibility of facing up to this problem when it is found that everyone wants them to go but no one wants to take them. A decision has to be made by somebody, and in the light of all the facts I can think of no better place to put those Japanese than in the ghost towns to which I have just referred. The climate there is comparatively good; the Japanese women and children will be treated well, and there will be ample protection. It should be remembered by hon. gentlemen that we are removing Japanese to other provinces, and we have had similar objections from certain quarters. But if this movement is to become effective in the most dangerous areas we must at times overlook some of the objections raised.
So far as I am personally concerned, as I said before I do not know of any better place than those ghost towns up in the Crow Valley to which these women and children might be moved. All facilities are available; it will be comparatively easy to carry on the education of the children, and all necessary sanitation and housing facilities are there. The houses need only a little repair, and when that is done those people will be out of harm's way. In view of the requests received and the investigations we have made I do not think that at this time we should be asked to change our decision in the matter.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. ILSLEY (Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
subtopic: CONCESSION TO ENCOURAGE PROSPECTING FOR BASE METALS AND STRATEGIC MATERIALS
speechtext:
I should like to make a brief announcement of a tax concession which will be contained in the budget and which is designed to encourage prospecting in Canada for base metals and strategic materials. Certain of these metals, such as tungsten, chromite, molybdenum and manganese, for example, are vitally necessary in our war equipment and in manufacturing processes. The demand for them may increase sharply. Some present sources of supply hinge upon precarious ocean transportation. We must cut down wherever possible the risk of failure of supply. It is more than possible that we have undiscovered sources of these metals right under our very door-steps. It would be inexcusable to neglect this possibility, and the government has decided to assist in the search for these metals.
The tax concession, -which will be available to both individuals and corporations, will be in the form of an allowance against income for income and excess profits tax purposes in respect of amounts contributed to prospecting syndicates registered with provincial authorities. A person may not claim an allowance of more than $500 in respect of any one syndicate, and there will be an over-all limit of $5,000 on the total amount which one person may claim/ This would allow a person to participate up to $500 in each of ten syndicates. These allowances will be subject to the provision that in no case shall the tax saving to any person by reason of the allowance exceed 40 per cent of the amount of deductions. In addition, in registered prospecting syndicates it is proposed to allow mining companies and bona fide exploration companies a deduction up to $5,000 for

expenditure in sending out their own prospectors. This allowance shall also be subject to the 40 per cent limitation on tax saving previously referred to.
The syndicates and companies would be required to satisfy the Minister of National Revenue that they had been actively engaged in prospecting for the metals and minerals in question under qualified persons during a substantial part of the 1942 season, and in the case of syndicates that they had carried out the purpose for which they were formed. An audited statement of expenditure will be required. These tax concessions will be given for one year only and will apply in respect of income for 1942. I am making this statement now because this prospecting should begin at once.

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENTS OF $5,000 AND UPWARDS

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speakeroldname: Hon. J. G. GARDINER (Minister of Agriculture) :
subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO PAYMENTS OF $5,000 AND UPWARDS
speechtext:
Yesterday I agreed that when we
reached the orders of the day I would give certain information with regard to payments under the wheat acreage reduction plan. With your permission, Mr. Speaker, and the permission of the house, if I may give this information without prejudice or without setting a precedent for the bringing down of lists of names in answer to questions on matters of this kind, I should like to give this information now.
The information desired is with regard to the persons who received payments of $5,000 and upwards under the wheat acreage reduction plan. It will be recalled by the house that under the regulations of last year provision was made for payment to any person who reduced his wheat acreage in the western provinces in the year 1941 as compared with an established acreage for the year 1940. There were seven cheques issued which exceeded $5,000 in amount, and the information desired was the names of the persons to whom these payments were made and their addresses.
The first name on the list which I have in my hand is Mrs. Marie Wilson, of Harris, Saskatchewan. The total decrease of wheat acreage made on the farms of Mrs. Wilson was 3,170 acres. The total number of acres of the reduced acreage that was placed in coarse grains was 977, which at $2 per acre amounted to $1,954; and in summer-fallow, 2,193 acres at $4, which amounted to $8,772, or a total of $10,726.
The second on the list is the Canada Permanent Mortgage company. The payments made appear on the list as having been made through the Regina office, although I think the head office of this company is in Toronto. This payment covers 218 farms located throughout the prairie provinces which I think are operated under a central organization that has been set up by the Canada Permanent Mortgage company. It is not for any one single farm. The total reduction in acreage made by the company

War Expenditures-Mr. Blackmore
on these farms was 20,320 acres. Coarse grains were seeded to 9,047 acres, which at $2 per acre made a total of SIS,094; summer-fallow, 11,273 acres, which at $4 amounted to $45,092, or a total on the 218 farms of $63,186.
The next name on the list is G. H. Wesley, of Wrentham, Alberta. I am not familiar personally with the facts of this case. I do not know whether Mr. Wesley is an individual farmer or a man who operates a farm on a company basis, but the payment was made to Mr. G. H. Wesley, of Wrentham, Alberta. The number of acres put into coarse grains was 615, which at $2 amounted to $1,230; grass, 50 acres at $2, amounting to S100; summer-fallow, 3,145 acres at $4, or $12,580, making a total of $13,910 for a wheat acreage reduction of 3,810 acres.
Next on the list is Noble Farms Ltd., Nobleford, Alberta. The number of acres put into coarse grains was 149, which at $2 amounted to $298; summer-fallow, 2,635 acres at $4, $10,540, or a total of $10,838 for a reduced wheat acreage of 2,784.
J. T. Heninger, Lucky Strike, Alberta, put into grass 138 acres, which at $2 amounted to $276; summer-fallow, 1,441 acres at $4, or $5,764, making a total of $6,040 for a total wheat acreage reduction of 1,479.
H. Newfeld, of Lethbridge, Alberta, put into summer-fallow 2,250 acres, which at $4 amounted to $9,000. His wheat acreage reduction was 2,250 acres.
Wm. Kynock, of Maybutt, Alberta, put into coarse grains 805 acres, which at $2 amounted to $1,610; summer-fallow, 1,793 acres at $4, or $7,172, making a total of $8,782 for a total wheat acreage reduction of 2,598 acres.
