speechtext: Mr. Speaker, that matter is being carefully considered, I may say.

The house resumed, from Wednesday, April 29, consideration of the motion of Mr. Mackenzie King for the appointment of a committee on war expenditures.
Mr. J. Ii. BLACKMORE (Lethbridge): Mr. Speaker, when the debate was adjourned yesterday I was giving some attention to the apparent duties of the committee according to the somewhat indefinite wording which I find in the resolution, and making suggestions as to how the committee's effectiveness might be improved. I should like briefly to refer to one item which I did not take time to cover yesterday, and after that I shall be done with this question. I refer to the words:
-to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein,
As these words stand, they are capable of an exceedingly wide interpretation. If I understand aright, the government's policy is to have a total war effort. In order to have a total war effort a great many things
2010	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Mr. Blackmore
require attention in Canada which at the present time are not being considered. I do not suppose the Prime Minister has in mind the inclusion of all the subjects which could properly occupy the attention of the committee, but may I just suggest one. In order to have a total war effort it is extremely necessary that we should have a high degree of morale in the country. While this is not the place to discuss the question-I intend merely to refer to it very briefly-matters of this kind ought to come before some committee somewhere. I have in mind the question of non-pensioned veterans' war widows. This properly comes under the scope of other committees, but it is not specifically pointed out what this committee shall cover, and the war widows have been presenting their case for a good deal of time now. When veterans who are receiving war veterans' allowance die, the widows, no matter in what condition they may be, according to the information I have, are deprived of the income. The result is that we are causing a great many people in Canada to feel exceedingly unhappy, and that unhappiness is spreading in a way which is not building up the morale of the people at home or of the troops.
That is just one matter. I referred yesterday to the fact that the committee's duties might easily involve the consideration of the production of food and clothing and many other things. However, in the interests of cutting short the discussion so that the government may go on with its business, I will defer until some other time anything else I may have to say.

Mr. Speaker, when the hon. member for Rose-town-Biggar (Mr. Coldwell) was speaking yesterday afternoon he mentioned that the war expenditures committee had not investigated any of the war contracts. It was my understanding, as I looked across at the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), who was chairman of that committee last year, that he did not agree with that point of view and insisted that war contracts had been investigated. Now I have every Tegard for the minister, but, so far as my observation goes I must disagree with him. I was on the committee during the session of 1941, and no contracts were investigated at that time- that is, up to June 3. I was not present at the sittings of the committee between July 7 and August 21, but my reading of the report leads me to believe that no specific contracts were examined. Yesterday the Department of Munitions and Supply was specifically mentioned, and my understanding is that the
fMr. Blackmore.]
chairman of the committee at that time said that contracts were investigated. I must repeat that while I was attending the sessions of the committee, contracts were not investigated. We did investigate the procedure. We had the deputy minister of the Department of Munitions and Supply before us, and I really believe, in view of all the circumstances, we expended too much time on acquiring information on the procedure followed from the time the Department of Munitions and Supply gets a request for material from any of the other departments. If my interpretation of the department's function is correct, it is largely a purchasing department. Orders do not initiate within that department; they come from some other department. I was on subcommittee No. 3, of which the Minister of National War Services was chairman. All our time was taken up with the investigating of the financial controls and the financial set-up in the various branches of the armed forces. I believe that the work was worth while and that good did accrue from it.
I have in my hand the report which was tabled on November 3 of last year. From a reading of it I cannot see that any contract as such was investigated by any of the subcommittees or by the committee as a whole. Subcommittee No. 1 dealt with precisely the same matters while it sat during the recess as it did while the house was in session-that is, contracts for civilian flying clubs, associations or companies, airports, aerodromes or air force building construction, specification or design, or such projects or inspection thereof during construction.
While the methods of calling for tenders and such things were examined, no specific contract was examined, so far as I can find. The paragraph in the report of this subcommittee dealing with those contracts reads as follows:
The subcommittee finds that great care is exercised to assure secrecy of bids and assure competitive bidding. The subcommittee finds contracts are let on a lump sum basiB or on a unit basis depending upon the nature of the work to be done. The subcommittee also finds that where all of the tenders are considered to be too high the contract is not awarded until tenders are again called for. In every instance the contract is av'arded to the lowest bidder. Before the contracts are awarded the whole project is checked by the timber controller's office and the tenders are also submitted to the defence department interested for its approval. The subcommittee finds that the construction branch of the Department of Munitions and Supply _ is very efficiently managed and that precautions are taken to protect the public interest. During the year 1940 something over 92 million dollars worth of buildings were constructed.

War Expenditures-Mr. Maclnnis
This is clear proof that it was not the specific contracts that were examined, but the method and the procedure by which contracts were let.
Then what did the committee do?

Just what I said; it examined procedure. And there may have been a great deal to do in that regard. I want it to be quite clear that I am not finding fault with what the committee did;
I am simply pointing out what the committee did not do, and it needs to be done.
Subcommittee No. 2 dealt with the matter of medical, dental and hospital services, also I believe with the matter of salvage and such things. Subcommittee No. 3 dealt with precisely the same matters as we dealt with when the house was in session last spring and summer. The three parts of the report are as follows:
Part 1 deals with the recommendations and principles enunciated in the interim report of former subcommittee No. 3.
Part 2 deals with the recommendations by the subcommittee in the light of the evidence submitted to it.
Part 3 deals with the evidence before the present subcommittee. It is an insight of the financial controls and checks operating within the Department of National Defence.
These are the matters that were investigated during the time the committee sat in 1941. While it was desirable to do this as a preliminary, I think a wider and more specific investigation should be carried out. It is more than time that we had a specific investigation of contracts, if for no other reason than to allay the suspicion that all is not well in our war production.
I think almost everyone admits the need for this committee. The Prime Minister, when proposing the committee to the house last year, stressed the desirability of having such a committee functioning. But there is a contradiction between this admission and the reluctance to start the committee going and the seeming hesitancy about having it investigate these very important matters. It is most desirable that the committee meet this year without delay. It should investigate and report on specific contracts that may be brought to its attention so that the public may be assured that no one is making financial gain out of the distress of the people at this time. A further function would be a continuation of what we did last year in regard to promoting thrift and efficiency in the organization and handling of our war production.
As was pointed out yesterday by the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas), such reports and such scrutiny would have an important effect on the morale of the people of this country.
It cannot be denied that in the setting up of war organizations and war boards almost the whole control has been put in the hands of big business and its representatives. This is a standing disgrace to the government. I wonder if this government remembers the investigation that was made by a committee of the house in 1934 into the activities of business organizations in Canada. Do they remember what was brought out and not contradicted? Have they forgotten the price spreads commission? I have under my hand a typical case of the kind of appointments made to responsible positions. Someone forwarded to me a press clipping from New Westminster referring to the appointment pi a man to a position in the Royal Canadian Air Force. The headline reads:
Byron Johnson gets R.C.A.F. building post.
The item gives Mr. Johnson's biography. Let me read it:
Byron Johnson of New Westminster has been appointed representative of Hon. C. G. Power, air minister, in connection with the building of new air bases forming part of Canada's air defence programme, the Royal Canadian Air Force announced yesterday.
Mr. Johnson will act as technical adviser to the minister and deputy minister, S. L. de Carteret, reporting directly to Ottawa on the progress of various aerodromes and buildings in course of construction for the R.C.A F., particularly in western Canada.
Here are his qualifications:
Mr. Johnson has been loaned to the dominion government by the firms with which he is associated. He is managing director of Gilley Brothers, Limited, and vice-president and director Evans, Coleman and Gilley Brothers, Limited, of New Westminster.
One of these is a fuel company and the other deals in lumber and building materials.
He has had long experience in operation of quarries, gravel pits, dredges and towboats and in the contracting industry.
Evidently this man's experience in dredging, quarries, tugboats and such things has eminently fitted him to be a supervisor of the building of airports. This is something that is continually going on, and it is sapping the morale of the people of Canada, to the extent that almost every person you meet is so cynical that people are just ready for anything. When people get to the state that they say nothing matters, then nothing does matter; they are ready for fascism or for anything that may come. This is what



War Expenditures-Mr. Maclnnis
happened to the people in many parts of Europe. They lost faith in their government; they took the attitude that things could not be any worse than they were. It was not true, of course; things could be worse, but things were so bad that the people believed that when they were told it.
Then we have the investigations that are taking place in the United States into what the Standard Oil people have been doing. These matters have appeared in Canadian newspapers, and people realize that there is a very close association not only between big business in Canada and big business in the United States but between big business all over the world. According to the New Statesman and Nation, of London, under date of April 4, in the course of evidence given by the representative of Standard Oil this came out:
Later in the year Standard Oil made arrangements with Mitsui of Japan, because, as it delicately put it, "As we fear the U.S. government, in the near future, may have grounds for action unfavourable to American and British trade, we consider it timely to organize with our Japanese partners."
In other words these representatives of big business realized that if hostilities broke out between the United States and Japan there would be a blockade, and they were getting ready to break the blockade. Let us remember also the evidence that came out after the last war with regard to the Briey iron mines in France, which were neither bombed nor attacked by artillery during the entire period of the war, and in which British, German and French investment was recognized and respected by all the belligerents.
These are facts which we must keep in mind. I suggest that this committee get to work as quickly as possible, and look into specific contracts. I doubt if there is a member of this house, at least on the opposition side, who has not had a number of contracts drawn to his attention in connection with which everything does not seem to be quite right. These contracts should be brought before the committee and investigated in every detail. I am satisfied that such an investigation will have a good effect upon the morale of our people, and will enable us to fight this war to a successful conclusion.

Mr. Speaker, I was a member of the committee that was set up last year, and I attended its meetings not only while the house was sitting but also during a portion of the time it sat during the recess. I have a few suggestions to offer which occurred to me during the sittings of the committee, as well as certain criticisms in regard to the set-up of
{.Mr. Maclnnis.]
the committee. I am one of those who believe the committee had a great work to do, and I think the challenge to do that work is still before the members of the committee which will function during the present session, to contribute something worth while to reassure the people of Canada and to increase the morale of this nation.
At the outset I must frankly say as a member of that committee that I do not believe the committee discharged the responsibility which was placed upon it. I was on the subcommittee that dealt with air matters; with contracts with civilian flying clubs, associations and companies, and also with army, navy and air force buildings, construction, and so on. With regard to my relationship to the other members of the committee, I shall always look back upon it as a very happy experience. Let us look at the number of contracts that have been awarded since the outbreak of this war. I do not know the figure at the moment, because there has been no statement by the Department of Munitions and Supply since last September as to the number of contracts let. This committee, which was at least suggested in the fall of 1940, during last session sat for a period of only six weeks, during which time it was actually in session for a matter of only some thirty to forty hours in all. Then last summer, when the committee sat during the recess, the three subcommittees had a total of only eighty-three meetings. Subcommittee No. 1 had 29 sittings and called 49 witnesses. That was the subcommittee on which I served for part of the summer, until it became necessary for me to leave in order to attend to certain personal matters. During the entire period of my absence, however, the chairman was kind enough to have forwarded to me copies of the evidence that was taken, so that I know what was actually done while I was away. Subcommittee No. 2 had 29 sittings, and 15 witnesses appeared before it. Subcommittee No. 3 held 25 sittings and called 25 witnesses. In other words last summer these three subcommittees had a total of 83 sittings. The average length of a sitting was not over two or two and a half hours, but make it three hours, if you will. The committee which was set up by parliament to investigate the billions of dollars' worth of contracts that have been let sat in the aggregate since its inception for a total of not more than 280 hours.
That will give you the picture, Mr. Speaker. That will tell you whether it would have been possible to look into any contracts whatever. Personally I do not know of any individual contracts that were inspected and examined

War Expenditures-Mr. Diejenbaker
during the time I sat on subcommittee No. 1. We did study the question of the awarding of general contracts by which the training at air observer schools and elementary flying training schools was placed in the hands of civilian companies. That was all we did in so far as the matter of contracts is concerned, and a little later I am going to deal with the results of our work in that connection.
The recommendations made by the committee appeared in the Votes and Proceedings of November 3, 1941, and comprise some sixty or seventy pages. They represent findings based on the essence of the evidence that was taken; but to-day not a member of this parliament knows whether any of these recommendations has ever been carried into effect, and as yet we have not had an opportunity of discussing them. It was on November 3, 1941, that the Minister of National War Services placed these recommendations of the subcommittees on the table of the house. Yet to-day, months later, there is not an hon. member who has any idea whether all our work, short as it was and incomplete as it necessarily would be having regard to the scope of the task and to the all too few hours we spent on it, or whether any portion of the findings, the essence of which is to be found in the records of the said Votes and Proceedings I have mentioned, has ever been looked at, or has even been considered by any department of government.
The tremendous field before us was and is enough to overwhelm. Hon. members will realize the extent of the work undertaken when I say that if the members of the committee had taken up the contracts which had been awarded before the committee was set up, and if we had sat twelve hours a day from the date the committee was first thought of, in November, 1941, and had taken a reasonable length of time in the consideration of each contract, we would now be approaching only one-eighth of the contracts which had been awarded up to that time. For this reason we believed that the proper approach was simply to take under consideration first the general scheme of awarding the contracts and to ascertain whether or not improvements could be suggested in connection therewith. It was manifestly impossible to go further than that. I would have appreciated being on the committee again this year, were it not for the fact that I believe, because this is one of the major committees of parliament, the duty of serving on it should be passed around to the various members of one's group. The problem is so tremendous that the mere mention that contracts were being awarded at the rate of fifteen hundred
44561-128J
a week when the committee commenced its sittings is enough to make anyone realize that it was not a public accounts committee where individual contracts could be looked into in particular.
We were not looking for scandal; we were not looking for wrongdoing. We had no opportunity to do so. Everything we did ascertain is concealed behind the secrecy established in the subcommittee on which I served.
Let us consider the set-up of the committee, and in that connection we might first consider the resolution forming it. I mention these points because frequently people will say, "Well, you have not shown any wrongdoing in connection with contracts awarded." In answer to that suggestion I reply that we never investigated any contracts, and I point out furthermore that we have no power to report to the house anything of an improper nature which may come to our attention.
The resolution reads:
Resolved that a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war-
I am in agreement that it is possible for the committee to investigate contracts in the Department of Munitions and Supply. I believe its powers are wide enough for that, and I agree with the view to that effect which was expressed yesterday by the Minister of National War Services. You can investigate, but how much can you report? The resolution continues:
-and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein.
In other words the only power we have is to investigate behind closed doors, and, having investigated, to report nothing but economies consistent with government policy. I point out, too, that when speaking on June 10 of last year in the house the Minister of National War Services explained that what took place in the committee was secret and that it could not be divulged, even to parliament-the parliament which had created the committee. At page 3751 of Hansard for June 10, 1941, I find this:
Mr. Thorson: I rise to a point of order. The committee decided that the sessions of subcommittees should be held in camera. I think that means that the evidence given before such committee must be regarded as privileged. If the rule is relaxed in respect of one statement, then the whole value of "in camera" sessions is gone. If it is permissible to refer to a statement of fact given in "in camera" sittings, then it would follow- that statements of expressions of opinion given in camera might also
2014	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Mr. Diejenbaker
be stated in this house. I suggest to your honour that the distinction should be this: If any evidence or any facts are available from a source other than statements made in camera,-
And I emphasize the word "other"-
-then such evidence or facts may be given in this house. But statements that are made in camera and expressions of opinion given in camera ought to be regarded as privileged. Otherwise the purpose of "in camera" sessions is completely defeated.
So that the chairman of the committee, a minister of the crown, has stated that the proper view to take of the evidence placed before the committee is that it is entirely secret and cannot be referred to. Of the evidence given before the subcommittee, of which I was a member, there was not a line, not a word which by the greatest stretch of the imagination could have been considered as of possible benefit to the enemy. But there was evidence placed before that subcommittee which it was our duty and responsibility to place before parliament and the country, to the end that the people might be in a position to judge whether or not the system in effect of granting to civilian companies the right to turn out men for service in the air force of Canada is a proper one.
One objection I took at that time, and which I now repeat, is that if the committee is to be worth while, if it is to canalize the war effort of the nation by improving the morale and by making the people realize there is nothing wrong, while at the same time digging fearlessly to find out any wrongdoing, then the size of the committee should be extended. It is too small now, and is too overwhelmingly composed of members supporting the government.
I realize that in a time of peace there are certain regulations with respect to committees providing for distribution based on party membership in the house. Mr. Speaker, these are no ordinary times; this was no ordinary committee. I repeat my suggestion to the Prime Minister this year to do something he refused to do last year, namely to equalize representation on the committee so that we may have equal representation, with the exception of the chairman, the vice-chairman and the chairmen of the subcommittees. If that were done all of us could go to work in the committee realizing that there are no political considerations whatsoever, and we could work together to the end sought by the Truman committee of the United States 
senate, when it gave a unanimous opinion, irrespective of party, and when, summing up its activities, stated its aim to be that
The committee, however, wants the war to be won as soon as possible

That is the purpose of this committee.
-and at a minimum expenditure of life and property. Carelessness and inefficiency have already cost us a great deal and, if continued, can cost us much more, even though in the long run we will win the -war because of the sheer extent of our resources.
That committee was composed of members from both sides of the United States senate. It was not overwhelmingly Republican or Democrat. It handed down a report in the month of January to the United States senate which has resulted already in the saving of millions of dollars. I repeat that the membership of this committee should be equalized as nearly as possible between the opposition and the government. If the Prime Minister will not agree then I contend that there should be more subcommittees, that more members of this house should be given an opportunity of serving. In Great Britain there are seven committees-army, admiralty, air, supply, home defence, trade, agriculture, economic warfare, and finally a coordinating committee to coordinate the work of the other committees.
The private members of this house have asked for an opportunity to serve; therefore I contend that the size of this committee should be increased. It would then be possible to appoint a large number of subcommittees and would be enabled the better to attack this problem differently from the way we did last year because we had so few members. In my opinion the evidence given before this committee should be made available to the members of this house except in cases where the committee determines that it would not be in the public interest to do so. The secrecy of the evidence taken and thereby the concealment of the true situation from the people is something that I condemn and will continue to condemn. The secrecy of the proceedings is condemning this parliament before the people. Because of this secrecy people at home are saying that there must be something wrong. They are saying that this government has never made an admission of any shortcomings, and they realize that with the tremendous work that has been done, there must be some shortcomings. To-day the membership in this house is controlled entirely by the government of the day. It is a trend which has been accelerated during recent months; parliament w more and more being

War Expenditures-Mr. Diejenbaker
convened merely for the purpose of voting supply. The members of this parliament should be something more than voiceless vassals in connection with everything but the voting of supply. We have a right to know, the people have a right to know what is going on.
Following the results of the plebiscite, the Prime Minister the other day used some very significant words. I quote from page 1920 of Hansard:
The questions that will have to be considered are all important and fortunately all members of the ministry and members of the House of Commons are now free to speak their minds without its being assumed for a moment that they are bping influenced by any past commitments-
If the sentence stopped there it might have been all right, but it continues:
-or considerations other than those which bear immediately upon the questions they are discussing.
What other considerations can there be that would prevent members of this house from speaking their minds? When members of the opposition rise in their places to voice fair and honest criticism, I cannot see what justification there is for members of the government invariably to point out that the war effort is being harmed thereby. Continue that trend and you destroy the independence, of parliament.
Private members' days have been taken away. Why? Because there is an overwhelming majority supporting the government. Regardless of the fact that we insist on there being private members' days, these have been taken away. The right to place before parliament the things that we believe are necessary has been denied us. It was not denied in this chamber in the last war until 1918, just three or four months before the end of the war. The other day I looked up the records and I find that in 1916 private members debated such matters as the civil service, divorce reform, liquor restrictions, labour bureaux, wheat marketing, and women's suffrage. In 1917 such matters were debated on private members' resolutions as granting the franchise to women and the establishment of a department of physical welfare. In 1918 the coal policy was debated. As it should, the war took up then as now a large portion of the time, but I see no reason why private members' days should be denied, or at least should not be allowed in a restricted sense.
When the opposition asks questions to-day it is invariably met with the answer that it is not in the public interest to give the information asked for. Only yesterday the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) said
that it was not in the public interest to tell the people of this country what was being done with their money in connection with agricultural payments. To-day, when he gave the information asked for, he did so in a way that I think this parliament should not accept. He said that he gave it without prejudice or without setting a precedent. If this trend is continued, if private members' days are taken away, if we have secrecy in a committee set up by parliament, if there is the extinction of our right to ask questions, what justification will there be for this house?
The other day Your Honour ruled that it was not proper that a question should be asked before the orders of the day unless it was of immediate importance. That ruling was quite right, but I would point out that in the British House of Commons, where the war is much closer than it is here or has been during recent months, two or three times a week members are allowed to ask questions of the ministers and to cross-examine them upon their answers. We are asked to accept the principle that ministers of the crown can answer by saying that it is not in the public interest to give the information, when the only justification for such an answer is some reason other than matters of state. I suggest that members on all sides of this house should get up and demand that answers be given.
If this practice is continued, regardless of the attitude adopted by other members around me, I intend to oppose it. If we can be put off with the reply that it is not in the public interest to answer, then our position as members of parliament is a mere sham. If this trend continues, this parliament will become nothing more than a sounding-board of the nation. If we are denied information on the ground that it is not in the public interest, the time may not be far distant when parliament and this country will be permitted to hear only the things and secure only the information which sounds well to the government, which in the opinion of the government will be to its interest to reveal. Against that I protest. The refusal to give information asked for from time to time is a serious infringement upon our parliamentary rights. I was glad to-day to find that three questions I had asked two or three days ago were answered. If the government would follow that example and provide us promptly with answers to the questions that are asked, there would not be so much objection to their not answering questions in the house on the orders of the day.
I protest against the secrecy of the war expenditures committee. Findings were made
2016	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Mr. Diefenbaker
with some of which I disagree and I wish to take this opportunity to refer to some of the findings with which I disagree, for the reason that as yet we have not had the opportunity to discuss them which was promised us by the Prime Minister at the time the findings were brought down.
I was not present when the various findings of my subcommittee were made, and other members of the committee were not present. I point out that the recommendations made here are based upon the evidence that was taken before the committee, but I dissociate myself from the conclusions based on some of the evidence referred to herein.
The report sets out the number of flying training schools in Canada and the number of air observer schools-22 elementary flying training schools and 10 air observer training schools. These schools have on their shoulders the responsibility of turning out pilots and observers for the Royal Canadian Air Force, or at least of contributing to the training that leads to the final graduation of the pupils entering these schools. This system of turning over to a private company or to civilian corporations the training of the members of one branch of the military forces of the nation is not followed in Great Britain. A system somewhat along this line existed until the outbreak of the war, but when war came the stand taken by the British government was that there was no justification for training men for the army or for the tanks or for aircraft or other of the armed services in civilian schools operated by civilians for the profit of civilians. The report says, at page 551, referring to the elementary flying training schools:
They are highly efficient and are carrying on their task without any thought of profits to the company or to private individuals; but the subcommittee also finds that under the great pressure of war work sufficient care has not been taken to safeguard the public interest as to what may happen in regard to profits after the war and when the war incentive will have ceased to exist.

What page is my hon.
friend reading from?

From page 551,
the last sentence of paragraph 4. The elementary flying training schools in the main were set up and sponsored by flying clubs throughout the dominion. Very good salaries are paid to the operators. Those who put up the capital, $35,000 being the capital, receive 5 per cent, and if there is a surplus at the end of the war it is to accrue to the flying clubs in the interests of civil aviation. There were no controls, to speak of, which would have assured that these moneys would

go to the flying clubs when the investigation commenced and last summer recommendations were made to prevent the shareholders of the elementary flying training schools from taking over the profit after the war, when patriotic incentive might very well tend to disappear. I think this house and the country has a right to know whether that recommendation of the committee was put into effect. Paragraph 5 of the committee's report says:
The subcommittee recommends that all of the common stock of all elementary flying training companies should be held in trust for the flying clubs sponsoring the companies, and that in no instance should any individual be permitted to hold the beneficial interest of any common stock other than the qualifying shares of directors and that a declaration of trust should be taken with respect to these shares.
Was that done? Has anything been done along that line? As yet we have no information in that regard.
Have you asked for it?

At the moment I
am dealing with the fact that the information has not been given.
This is the first opportunity to give it. You have not asked for it before.

I shall be making
further remarks with which my hon. friend may not agree, and he can make his speech when I have finished.
The committee recommended that the profit of 50 cents per flying hour received by the company should be reduced to 25 cents. Parliament met after that, and we were assured that that reduction had been made. Yet when our committee met in July and August of last year we found that these reductions had not up to that time been accepted and adopted.
At page 554 of the report the subcommittee recommended:
That all profits should be invested in noninterest bearing Dominion of Canada bonds so that all profits earned will be available for war purposes until the end of the war. Most of the companies are already following this practice. The subcommittee has already recommended that the agreement should be amended making this compulsory.
Parliament has a right to know whether or not this recommendation was carried into effect.
I come now to what I consider is a subject of fair criticism, namely the establishment of air observer schools under civilian operation in this country. There are ten of them. These schools have received contracts from the government to train airmen as observers. The companies are capitalized at

War Expenditures-Mr. Diejenbaker
150,000, and there is no limitation whatsoever on the profits which the companies are making. They are purely private companies. These companies have none of the justifications for their existence that the elementary flying training schools have, except in the results they achieve. I submit that the time has come when in the interests of the war effort of this nation the air observer schools should be taken over by the dominion and not be operated by civilian companies. At the present time these companies operating the air observer schools receive a management fee of $2,700 per month, and any saving they make on that basis goes to the operating company. In the matter of operation and maintenance, which includes salaries for pilots, engineers, electricians, mechanics, and so on, the agreement calls for the payment of a monthly target price, which in the first agreement was set at $17,500. The agreement also provides for a revision of the target price to make adjustment for changes made from time to time in the training syllabus. It further provides that every twenty-four weeks the target price will be revised in the light of existing costs and that any balance on hand in this account at the conclusion of the contract-and most of these contracts will end in March of 1943-will be divided on the basis of 75 per cent to the crown and 25 per cent as profit to the company.
Finally, there is provision for the payment of one dollar profit for every flying hour flown during the period.	The committee recommended that that said amount be reduced to thirty-five cents. As yet we have no information as to whether this has been done. There is one item in the report which I challenge. At page 556 it is stated:
The subcommittee has carefully considered the question of profits which will be earned by the operating companies. Partly on account of highly efficient management and partly on account of the pupil intake as fixed by the contract being increased without proportionate increase in management costs it was found that substantial profits were being earned.
It will be noted that this finding is surrounded by a good deal of explanation before you get to the fact, that "substantial profits were being earned". Then it says:
The following examples of lunar monthly-profits from one of the schools show an average profit of $1,112:
Example No	1	
$1,176Example No.	2	
1,340Example No.	3	
819
This company is awarded a contract by the government to train men for the armed services, and even on the basis of this report
would be making a yearly profit of $14,456, "under favourable conditions". I challenge, Mr. Speaker, the right of the members of the committee who drafted this report to reveal only part of the story and not the whole story; I challenge their right to try to explain away the very large profits at the air observers' schools which the operating companies are receiving. I do not know whether this is No. 1 or not, because there is no indication as to which it is, but I think this is the company which, in addition to showing the net profit here stated, paid to its parent company during one year $15,658.32 over and above what they showed as profit earned. In other words during the period of the first year this company made approximately $30,000, but was able, by showing payments to the parent company, to show that its profit was in fact less.
On what account were the payments?

The minister asks, on what account. The payments were made to cover experience and responsibility on the part of the parent company, experience having been gained by its operations during the days of peace, and the other item for its responsibility to return the goods placed in charge of the company.
And services. The hon. member has omitted a very important matter.
My hon. friend may explain this.
I rise to a point of order. My hon. friend is referring to evidence given in secrecy and to matters not included in the report.
Just as you did.
I was stopped, and I am suggesting that the hon. member should be stopped. It is not fair. He is giving only half the picture.
He is telling what you do not want to hear.
I do not think that that is a point of order.

Mr. Speaker, I object,
and I ask for a ruling as to whether the hon. member who is speaking has the right to quote from secret evidence.

He is
quoting from the report.
2018	COMMONS
War Expenditures-Mr. Diejenbaker

No, it is not in the report. What my hon. friend is referring to, is services rendered by the parent companies, and this is not mentioned in the report. If he wanted it in the report he should have been there when the report was prepared and asked that it be put in.
There is no point of order.
I must press for a ruling, Mr. Speaker.

As a matter of fact the question has been raised before with regard to what was said in secret not being available to the house. I believe I then ruled that the hon. member for Halton (Mr. Cleaver) who has now spoken and who has raised the point of order could not refer to matters which were secret as before the committee, and he accepted the ruling and did not do so. With reference to the hon. member for Lake Centre who is now speaking, I did not know that he was alluding to something which was in a secret paper.
He was replying to a question of the minister.
That is not fair. He made the statement before the minister asked him.

I asked him, what
account? I am just as ignorant as my hon. friend is; I was following the report and chasing down to find where the figure was which the hon. member had mentioned.

My time has
elapsed, but may I conclude with just one reference, because I do not want to go beyond my time. There are ten of these air observers' schools in Canada, and the time has come when they should be taken over by the government and profits should not be permitted to continue to accrue to -private companies which operate the schools.
I point out in conclusion, Mr. Speaker, that most of these schools are owned to-day by a great corporation, or should I say an auxiliary of a great transportation corporation -not the Canadian National Railways, which so far as I know has no interest in any of them. The time has come to take over these schools, and to take the profit away from private individuals in connection with training men for armed services. The government should take over these schools so that when the war is over Canada as a nation will be in a position to extend and develop her air services in all parts of the world.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. T. THORSON (Minister of National War Services):
speechtext:
At the outset I should like to express regret that the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) will not be a member of the war expenditures committee this session. He did excellent work in the subcommittee of which he was a member, he contributed valuable criticism to the work of that subcommittee, and the vigour of his presentation was very helpful indeed.
The fourth report of the war expenditures committee last session recommended that the inquiry should be continued and that a committee should be set up this session for that purpose. Indeed, the work of such a committee as this can never be concluded; there will be plenty of work for a body of this kind as long as the war lasts.
Last year there was no restriction whatsoever upon the activities of the committee. I so stated yesterday; I also said that there would be no restriction upon the activities of the committee this year. The whole field of war expenditures is open to the committee for investigation for the purpose of recommending what economies are possible in connection with war expenditures consistent with government policy in the matter.
But nothing else.

That is the function of this particular committee. The committee in the course of its sittings last session laid dowrn certain fundamental principles. Some of them were referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre a few minutes ago. It was, I think, generally agreed that the war expenditures committee is not a public accounts committee and is essentially different in its functions from a public accounts committee. I think there was general agreement among all the members of the committee to that effect.
For example, it is not a primary function of the war expenditures committee to examine a particular transaction or to investigate charges in respect of a transaction.
That is the point of disagreement.
I think there was general agreement in the committee last year on that subject.
I never agreed that that was not a function of the committee.
Do they not examine contracts in England?

I was very careful to point out that it is not a primary function of

War Expenditures-Mr. Thorson
this committee to examine any particular transaction or any past transaction or to investigate any particular charges. The function of this committee is to recommend economies that may be possible. In order to enable it to recommend such economies it may have to go into particular transactions and examine them, but there is an essential difference between the functions of such a committee as this and the functions of a public accounts committee. May I say that it is open to any hon. member to bring any particular transactions before the public accounts committee. He may move that a particular transaction be referred to the public accounts committee. But I think it will be agreed that there is an essential and fundamental difference between the purposes of this committee and those of the public accounts committee.
This is the public accounts committee for war expenditures.

Similarly any account, any contract, any transaction may be referred by any hon. member to the public accounts committee; he may move that any particular transaction go to the public accounts committee. That is his prerogative and his right.
Similarly it was agreed that this committee is not primarily a fact-finding committee.
Then it is utterly useless.
No, it is not utterly useless. The work this committee did last year was exceedingly valuable-
The money spent on it was utterly useless, if that is all it produces.
-and was instrumental in bringing about a good many economies, as I shall elaborate as I proceed.
Does the minister believe that the function of this committee is to examine the expenditures?
Yes.
Then does he not think the committee has to make the examination by looking into the transactions?
They may-
They should.

-and they will. If the hon. member will allow me to continue, he will see that the work of the committee proceeded in an orderly manner, first, for the purpose of ascertaining what controls and checks there were, then to indicate what controls and checks there ought to be; then the
intention was that the committee would move from such inquiries into any particular transactions that the committee wished to investigate. I think hon. members will see the plan upon which the committee operated and the sound reasons that lay back of that plan of procedure.
I think it was agreed that the committee is not primarily a fact-finding committee. It could not possibly examine the hundreds, the thousands of war contracts individually. If it had started in with the examination of individual contracts, it could not have accomplished the functions for which it was designed.
The committee is not restricted, as the British committee is, to the examination of present expenditures, it may loot into past expenditures, but its purpose in looking into past expenditures is to ascertain what economies might be possible for the future.
The wording of the reference, which is exactly the same as the reference in the case of the British committee, subject to what I have just said, is that the committee should "examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein."
Therefore primarily the committee is an economy recommending committee. That, I think, makes its functions essentially different from those of a public accounts committee or those of any special committee that may be set up for the ascertainment of any particular sets of facts.
The committee is the master of its own procedure; it is also the master of its subjects of inquiry. It consists entirely of private members; no member of the government is on the committee; there are no governmental instructions to the committee; the reference is as broad as it is possible to devise. There were no restrictions upon its activities last year; there are no restrictions upon its activities this year.
Last year when the committee opened its inquiry it held open sittings. Six sittings were devoted to the Department of Munitions and Supply for the purpose of ascertaining the manner in which that department functioned, the manner in which it awarded contracts, the extent to which it awarded contracts on the basis of tenders, the extent to w'hich it departed from that basis in awarding contracts and the principles subject to which it awarded contracts on a basis other than by tender. We explored the organization of the department, the checks and controls that

War Expenditures-Mr. Thorson
existed in the department to see that matters were conducted with regularity and economy; we investigated such subjects as cost accounting in the department itself, the controls exercised by the comptroller of the treasury, the controls exercised by the joint inspection board of the United Kingdom and Canada, the controls exercised by the treasury board and by the auditor general.
Later, as subject after subject was brought to the attention of the committee, it became clear and obvious to every member of the committee that we must operate by subcommittees if we were to make the best use of the services of the members of the committee and cope with the tremendous volume of work that lay before the committee. That was essential. Consequently the committee resolved itself into three subcommittees, which sat during the period the house was in session and for six or seven weeks during the adjournment. When these subcommittees concluded their work, during the adjournment of the house, they made individual reports which were the basis of reports of the whole committee, which reports were all tabled on the reopening of parliament on November 3.
The fifth report dealt with contracts with civilian flying clubs, associations or companies; the sixth report with army, navy and air force buildings construction, specifications and designs for such projects, and the inspection thereof during construction; the seventh report with medical, dental and hospitalization services in the army, navy and air force; the eighth report with food and other supplies including miscellaneous services for the forces, the inspection and distribution thereof; the ninth report with the salvage of waste; the tenth report with such subjects as financial controls over army, navy and air force expenditures, and headquarters establishments in army, navy and air force.
All these reports indicate that the first subjects to be explored were activities which were initiated in the departments of national defence. There was a reason for this. The House of Commons sees the war appropriation bill for the first time when it is introduced in this house. The war appropriation is based upon estimates that come from the departments of national defence after going through a certain procedure; through the treasury board, to the war committee of the cabinet and to council. Then they become the basis for the appropriation bill which is submitted to parliament. But these estimates are themselves based upon war establishments, and it was thought that it would be wise to see what economies were possible in the defence departments, where these expenditures

originated. Therefore a great deal of our time last year was devoted to an investigation of checks and controls. I believe hon. members will find an excellent statement of the checks and controls in effect at the present time over army, navy and air force expenditures-

If the minister would permit an interruption, that was all academic. Did the committee, after some six or eight sessions, make any recommendation to improve or remedy conditions with respect to those checks and controls?
Yes.
What was that recommendation?

I pointed out that the estimates themselves are based upon war establishments. Perhaps the outstanding recommendation of the subcommittee which dealt with that particular subject was that there should be a war establishments committee in every defence department where such a committee did not already exist; furthermore, that a financial superintendent should be appointed in each of the defence departments where such an office did not already exist, and that such financial superintendent should be a civilian, responsible to the deputy minister and be a member of the war establishments committee. That was recommended on the ground that there was need for civilian authority and control in the matter of army, navy and air force expenditures; not on the assumption that there should be civilian authority over the service personnel, or service personnel superiority over the civilian authority, but with the idea that each should be in aid of the other and complementary to the other, so that the matter of financial control should not be restrictive of the war effort but in aid of it. That is why the committee adopted as its objective a certain purpose, namely, that the people of Canada should know that there was at Ottawa a committee of private members of parliament concerned with seeing that a dollar's worth of war effort should be given in return for every dollar contributed to the war effort by the Canadian people, either by way of taxation or by way of loan.
These recommendations to which I have referred have been adopted, actually or in principle. In respect of the appointment of a financial superintendent, there already was such an officer in connection with the army. Since our recommendations were made, a financial superintendent has been appointed in the Department of National Defence for Air, and a similar appointment is proposed

War Expenditures-Mr. Thorson
in connection with naval services. A war establishments committee was already operating in the army, and in November of last year, after our report was made, the financial superintendent was made a member of that committee. The principle has been adopted in the navy. In the case of the air force, a war establishments committee has been appointed, of which the financial superintendent has been made a member. I think these basic recommendations made by the committee will result in complete cooperation between the civilian authority and the service personnel in the matter of those controls and checks which are essential to the most efficient performance of the duties that are assigned to those departments.
In that regard I think a valuable contribution was made by this committee to the work of the defence departments, all three of which have expressed their appreciation of the assistance given by the committee in enabling them to put into effect the reforms that were recommended in the report, which reforms not only effect economies but promote efficiency in the departments as well. The primary purpose last year was to investigate that field of war expenditures that actually lay behind the war contracts, because it was in that field that the greatest economies were possible, and it was in that field that there was the greatest need for checks and controls.
A very full and complete statement of the existing checks and controls is contained in pages 627 to 643 of No. 15 of the minutes of proceedings of the special committee. This also appears at pages 585 to 601 of the Votes and Proceedings of November 3, 1941; I commend the reading of that statement to members of this house. They will see that we have a system of careful checks and controls of war expenditures, starting with the very origin of these expenditures.
They will understand the importance of the recommendations made by the committee in the matters of checks and controls. I am sure hon. members will be glad to see the manner in which the defence departments have acted in respect of these essential and fundamental recommendations of the war *expenditures committee.
The war expenditures committee having explored the checks and controls that are in existence, and having indicated the additional checks and controls that there ought to be, then it was a logical matter to go into specific transactions and specific departments. The war expenditures committee, having explored these fundamental and foundational
matters may now, with some understanding, go into the subject of war contracts and specific transactions generally. The committee may investigate any war departments, indeed any department of the government that receives war appropriations, and explore any of their activities connected with the war.
I suggest that there is reason in going about this exploration in an orderly manner. We have written into the record what I think is a valuable contribution to the system of checks and controls that there ought to be in the case of war expenditures. I think the committee may now usefully explore the activities of the Department of Munitions and Supply. Indeed, if I had been honoured with the chairmanship of the committee this year, as I was honoured last year, I would have suggested to the committee that the whole subject of war contracts should be made the subject of study during this session of the house. May I say this, that the government invites the closest scrutiny of any war contract and has no hesitation in extending that invitation. May I say again something I could not have said last year, on my responsibility as a member of the government, that there is no restriction whatsoever upon the activities of this committee. This is a committee charged with the duty of examining all war expenditures for the purpose of recommending economies. May I say further that if hon. members of this committee run into anything that they think should be referred, any member of the house has a right to move that such transaction be referred to the public accounts committee. That is a right any member has. It is open to any member to do that.
As we explored the subject of checks and controls last year, so the committee this year may study the subject of war contracts. I have no hesitation in saying that the Department of Munitions and Supply is one of the achievements of this government. It started off by being the central purchasing agent for all defence departments, after the awarding of contracts had been taken away from those departments. There was first of all the defence purchasing board, then the war purchasing board and, finally, the Department of Munitions and Supply. When the history of that department is written it will be one of the romances of the war effort of this country-and I say that without any hesitation at all. It started off as a central purchasing agent, but it has gone far beyond that. It is now also the controller of supplies. It has gone far beyond the simple function of being a central purchasing agent.

War Expenditures-Mr. Thorson
It has been instrumental in capital assistance. That is one subject that members of the committee should thoroughly and carefully explore. It has also set up a large number of government-owned companies for purposes of the war. Capital assistance has amounted to approximately half a billion dollars. There are eleven government-owned companies directly associated with the war effort. Their names, as set out at page 641 of the minutes of proceedings No. 15 of the special committee on war expenditures, are as follows:
Allied War Supplies Corporation
Federal Aircraft Limited
Research Enterprises Limited
Small Arms Limited
Wartime Housing Limited
Fairmont Company Limited
Melbourne Merchandising Limited
Plateau Company Limited
Citadel Merchandising Company Limited
Wartime Merchant Shipping Limited
War Supplies Limited.
The functions of these various government-owned companies are varied. Some of them are supervising companies; others are manufacturing or construction companies. Again, others are commodity procurement companies, while others are purchasing companies. To a very large extent the government has embarked upon public ownership of the production and procurement of munitions of war.
I suggest that these are all exceedingly interesting subjects for inquiry-the whole subject of war contracts; the whole subject of capital assistance; the whole subject of publicly-owned companies engaged in the war effort of the country.
Reference has been made to the matter of war contracts. There are thousands of these contracts. It would be a most stupid method of procedure to start in to examine each individual contract. There would be far more sense in examining the principles subject to which these contracts are awarded, the considerations governing the awarding of these contracts and the general principles involved, so as to indicate in what way there may be an improvement in the situation, from the point of view of economy and efficiency.
Approximately 95 per cent in number of all contracts awarded is by the tender system. But there are some purchases made where the tender system cannot be used; these purchases fall into the following categories, as detailed at page 640 of minutes of proceedings No. 15:
(a)	Where extreme military urgency requires immediate delivery.
(b)	Where the requirement is so large that the productive capacity of the entire industry must be harnessed.

(c)	Where the technical nature of the article required narrow's the field of supply to one or two sources.
(d)	Where, in the interests of military secrecy, it is considered unwise to give plans and specifications to more than one or two firms, such to be chosen because of their aptitude in this particular type of manufacture.
_ I know that some feeling has been created in the house because on a number of occasions the government has stated that it is not in the public interest to give certain information. We have given far more information than the British government has ever given. We are proud to be allies of Great Britain in this great conflict; the fact is that the British government has asked us not to give out information that we have been giving out. This is not done for the purpose of hiding anything. The government has nothing to hide. We can give this information to committees sitting in camera. I say again, if any member of this house thinks that a transaction ought to be referred to the public accounts committee, he can rise in his place and move to refer such transaction to that committee.
This raises the whole question of "in camera" proceedings. I do not know why members use the phrase "sitting in secret", when the proper phrase is "sitting in camera".
What is the difference?

There is a vast difference. The committee did not sit in camera for the purpose of hiding anything; it sat in camera for the purpose of finding out things. The British committee on war expenditures sat always in camera, both the committee of the whole and the subcommittees. There was not a single session of the British committee, either sitting as a whole or as subcommittees, that was held otherwise than in camera. There is no parliament anywhere in the world that is more jealous of its rights and prerogatives, or more deeply concerned with doing its duty than the British parliament. In this regard the British parliament is an excellent model and example for us to follow, as we follow the British house in so many respects.
How many sittings have they had in the last two years?

They have had a good many. A number of the recommendations made by the British committee have been in effect in Canada for a long time; it is only recently that the British government has been following some of the examples that we have set in the matter of a Department of Munitions and Supply, a central purchasing agency for all defence depart-

War Expenditures-Mr. Thor son
ments and so on. Our action will be also a model for the United States. They have acknowledged freely the value of the system that we have set up for the central purchasing and control of materials and commodities such as exists in our Department of Munitions and Supply.
There are arguments for sitting in camera as well as for sitting in open session. Last year we sat in open session part of the time, and in camera for most of the sittings of the subcommittees. The committee is completely master of its own proceedings; it can decide whether they shall sit in open session or in camera. The example of the British committee indicated the value of sitting in camera, and I express my own opinion as to the value of sitting in camera. There are arguments both ways, but I have not the slightest hesitation- in saying that the argument in favour of an inquiry of this sort sitting in camera is overwhelming.
I know there is value in having the press present and in having the proceedings open, but if the essential purpose is to make recommendations for economy, as is the purpose of this committee, then it can best discharge this duty by sitting in camera. It is not a matter entirely of secrecy, although all matters of secrecy must be carefully guarded. I do not put the case for sitting in camera on the basis of secrecy; that is only a small part of it. I put it on a much wider base, and I indicated that base in the speech I made in this house last session. I gave two reasons, and I put forward one of them quite frankly and without intending to give offence to anybody.
If members sit in camera they will give more direct and more concentrated attention to the subject that is at hand than they would if the sittings were in the open with the press present. There will be fewer speeches made by members; there will be fewer efforts made to catch the head-lines. When I make that statement, I intend it to be general and applicable to all members. If there is no press there, if there is no competition to make the head-lines, members will be inquiring into what is before them rather than making speeches about something. Making speeches does not advance an inquiry. An inquiry is something that must be made with undivided attention to the subject that is at hand. That is one point, but it is not the most important reason for sitting in camera.
This committee is charged with the duty of recommending economies. In order to discharge that duty intelligently it must get information from either service personnel or civilian members of the various departments
who have all the facts, who know all the surrounding details, who know whether economies are possible. Therefore it is necessary that there should be the freest and fullest interchange of opinion between those persons, whether service personnel or civilian, and members of the committee. Everyone who has had experience with parliamentary inquiries knows that you cannot have that full and free exchange of opinion-not statements of fact-except in confidence. It is only human for persons who are in the public service to freeze up when they know that everything they state, that every opinion they express may possibly be blazoned on the head-lines. There ought to be a free exchange of opinion, a mutual searching between the officers of the departments and the members of the committee for ways and means of effecting economies.
Let me say again that this is not a fact finding committee; this is a committee for the investigation of transactions, if you like, but for the purpose of recommending economies. There is another committee that can investigate particular transactions if it is felt that an investigation of such transactions should be made. I say again it is open to any member of the committee to move that a particular transaction be referred to a standing committee of this house, the public accounts committee.
The experience of that free exchange of opinion last year was splendid. It was valuable. It enabled the committee to recommend outstanding reforms, many of which have been put into effect and practised, with increased economies and increased efficiency resulting.
In the subjects that are before the committee this year, such as war contracts, there is the fullest possible scope for inquiry as to the various bases upon which contracts are awarded, when they are awarded otherwise than on the basis of tender. That opens a great field of inquiry, but a field that could not be fully or properly explored by sitting down and indiscriminately seeking to analyse all the facts of each individual contract. There has to be a certain amount of confidence in the fact that we have people in the department who are devoted servants of the public and are seeking to do their best.
So far as tenders are concerned, I should like to suggest to hon. members that they read the statement on checks and controls relating to war contracts and relating to purchasing in the Department of Munitions and Supply contained in pages 635 to 643 of volume No. 15 of the minutes of proceedings, and they will see what system of checks and controls there

War Expenditures-Mr. Thor son
is in that department. How can that system be improved to bring about economy? That is a first-class and important subject of inquiry.
Then there is the matter of capital assistance. Are the conditions subject to which capital assistance is granted satisfactory-and we have spent approximately half a billion dollars in capital assistance? Can the conditions be improved? Can economies be effected in that field? Similarly with respect to the operations of the eleven government-owned companies set up for the purpose of aiding this country in its war effort, are those operations being carried on satisfactorily? All of these subjects are open to the committee this year.
Last year, as I pointed out a moment ago, the committee adopted as its chief objective that its purpose should be to see that Canada should get a dollar's worth of war effort for every dollar contributed by the Canadian people. I think I can say that last year the committee did excellent work. It was concerned with results. Not one of the members of the committee sought to glorify himself. They could have brought in estimates of large amounts of proposed economies. They did not do so, but they brought forward recommendations that will result in tremendous economies, and economies that are possible without in any way reducing the efficiency of our war effort. All of the war departments of national defence have expressed their appreciation of the cooperation of the committee. The committee last year was a stimulating factor in the promotion of economy reforms. The very existence of the committee has an extremely salutary effect, for no war department knows when its affairs may be examined or its expenditures scrutinized. The committee may well follow up all of its recommendations of last year to inquire what progress is being made in implementing them where they have not already been adopted, because there is always a value in following up an inquiry of this sort.
The work of this committee is not easy. It is very difficult. It is also very interesting and exceedingly important. Of course there are differences of opinion, but I think they have been bona fide differences of opinion.
I think I may speak fully and freely when I say that the government invites criticism.
I have myself frequently expressed appreciation of the value of criticism, and on this first occasion to speak on this subject as a minister of the crown I invite criticism. Criticism is helpful. But there must also be an appreciation of certain fundamentals. There is a vast difference between giving out facts in this

house and giving information to a committee sitting in camera, and I am sure that members of the house on both sides will appreciate those fundamental differences.
Cooperation is essential; differences of opinion are unavoidable, and they are valuable because "it is only upon the anvil of discussion that the spark of truth is struck." I forget who was the author of that saying, but it is a very helpful one. We must have discussion. But at the same time we are engaged in a war effort in which every person in this country is vitally interested, and we must avoid giving information which may be of value to the enemy. Very frequently, again and again and again, for reasons which it cannot even properly give, the government is handicapped. It could answer certain criticisms easily if it felt that it could properly say certain things. But it often cannot safely make the answers without disclosing facts that should not be disclosed. While the government invites criticism, may I also suggest this, that members of the house extend a certain amount of confidence and faith in those who are engaged in this country's administration. I think they are entitled to that, and I believe that members of this house know they are entitled to have it. We would gladly give on the floor of the house the information asked for if we could properly do so, because I am satisfied that we have nothing to hide. Members of the committee, however, can get the fullest information. Members may not always be able to get information on the floor of the house for reasons of public policy, but I do not remember a single instance when a person came before the subcommittee, of which I was chairman, where information was refused. Sometimes the information was given off the record when it could not be given otherwise. There has to be cooperation, and a certain amount of faith and confidence in those who are charged with the administration. Let me assure you, Mr. Speaker, that we are just as deeply interested and concerned in the successful issue of this war effort as hon. members opposite are, and there is upon our shoulders a very heavy responsibility. .
On everybody's shoulders.

And upon everybody's shoulders. I believe that this committee can do a marvellous job. I think it did a fairly good job last year, although perhaps it is not for me to say so. I regarded it as a great privilege to be chairman; I was deeply appreciative of the cooperation that was given me from all sides. Differences of opinion-

War Expenditures-Mr. Johnston (Bow-River)
yes, but unity of purpose-likewise yes. I hope that when this committee sits again there will be that same unity of purpose in the discharge of a very difficult but very interesting and important task.
I hope that this motion will pass the house with unanimity.

In view of what the minister says of the marvellous job which has been done by this committee- and I agree with him-will he tell us why the committee was not set up at the beginning of the session rather than at this late date?
