After Recess
The house resumed at eight o'clock.

When the house rose I was discussing the apparently confused . operations of the war expenditures committee. It seems that there has been a great deal of confusion over the order of reference relating to this committee. It must be evident to the house that there should be a clarifying of this order of reference. I was interested in the remark of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) in regard to the Department of Munitions and Supply when he said it was one of the greatest achievements of the war. He pointed out that under this department something over a billion dollars had been spent in the setting up of government-owned industries. I think the minister is perfectly right in saying that the Department of Munitions and Supply is one of the most important departments of the government at this time. I have persistently maintained that that department, which controls the production of this country, is most important, and we should not overlook the fact that that department should have, shall I say, a thorough investigation, not that I am trying to imply that the minister in charge is inefficient in handling that department, but in view of the great importance of that department.
The Minister of National War Services also tried to differentiate between a secret session and a session held in camera. I agree with the greater part of that statement; I can see a decided advantage, if it is properly handled, in the committee itself sitting in camera, if it is clearly understood that when the report of the committee is brought back to the house and concurrence in that report is moved, the members of this house in secret session be allowed to go into every detail of the work that was carried on in the com-Jiittee. I do not think it is right that that committee should carry on its work in camera and the members of this house as representa-

tives of the people of Canada have absolutely no information as to what was going on. It is also a matter of note that members of this house are ignorant of what policies or recommendations of the committee were accepted by the government itself. I recall just lately one of the members who was on that committee stating that he did not know of one recommendation of the committee that was adopted by the government. That seems to make the committee useless.
I also note that in the entire work of the committee they had only eighty-three sittings. That does not seem to be anything approaching a thorough investigation of the problems set before that committee. The work was thought to be so voluminous that the committee divided itself into three parts, each part taking a separate portion of the work. But my understanding is that never did those three subcommittees sit at the same time, on the same day; the reason being that there was a shortage of reporting staff. That is rather shocking, when 3-ou think of a committee of that size going to all the trouble they did go to, staying here in Ottawa away from their own work during those six weeks; yet one of those committees at least had to sit idly by because the reporting staff was not large enough to. take care of the three subcommittees sitting together. Therefore it seems to have been useless to set up three subcommittees, especially when they worked only two or three hours a day.
I am not trying at all to belittle the work of the committee, because from reading the record I know that a great deal of strenuous work was carried on by it. Yet I am told that there was a great deal of confusion among the members of the committee themselves, not knowing where they were going. I hope that having had the experience of the past year's work in that regard, the Prime Minister will see to it that those difficulties are removed.
The work of the committee must necessarily entail a great deal of interviewing of officials from different departments to get the detailed information that the committee requires. But I cannot bring myself to believe that the committee will ever get anywhere unless it examines more thoroughly into the contracts, regardless of what the Minister of National War Services said, as chairman of that committee, that it was not a fact-finding committee. I really do not know what that term involves. He said it was not the function of the committee to investigate particular contracts. I think there will have to be a reexamination of the order of procedure of the whole thing.

War Expenditures-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
Giving all due credit to the members of the committee for the work they did and the laborious time they had, I often doubt whether the results were worth the efforts made. It may be recalled that, speaking in the house a couple of weeks ago, referring to this committee, I expressed the opinion that the scope of reference should be widened to include production and the organization of production. I am more convinced now than I ever was that that is our problem, and that is why I referred a moment ago particularly to the Department of Munitions and Supply. If we are going to win this war we must get rid of that inferiority complex, saying that we are doing well enough. When a question is put to a minister in regard to contracts with a certain company, the reply is usually, "Well, that company has more contracts now than it ever had in its history." That is no answer to the question at all. Surely to goodness in war time it should not be a matter of whether or not a company has more contracts than it ever had before. The point should be, is it producing to capacity; could it produce more if certain changes were made. Perhaps we have now reached the point where some headway can be made, for in my opinion that is the most important question confronting this nation at the present'time, and it seems to be the question that is most evaded.
I do not want to belittle the suggestion that the saving of money is important, but, after all, that is not my great concern at this time. I think money should be made the servant and not the master of this nation. I do not want to criticize the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) too severely, but I am quite convinced that he is not capable of carrying on the tremendous work of placing orders, checking those orders, checking costs and all the other work that is entailed in seeing that the production organization of this country is such that we can carry on at maximum capacity. The expression has often been used, even by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) himself, that we are doing a marvellous job, that we are producing 100 per cent to capacity. Certainly that is not correct, and I think it is the wrong sort of propaganda to be putting out to the country. The fact is that though I have visited a number of factories I have never found one which, in my opinion., was doing what it should be doing, that is, working to anywhere near capacity. For us to go out and tell this nation that we are producing to capacity is, in my opinion, breaking down the morale of the people. They have only to walk by the factories to see the situation. They see
some of them closing at five o'clock in the afternoon. They go by the employment offices in the cities and see hundreds of men unemployed. Finally they reach the point where they say, "Well, if the government is not more concerned about the safety of the empire than that, why should we worry?"
I have spoken to men working in certain factories. I have been told that the manager of a plant deliberately told his men that they must not work so quickly. One chap told me that the manager of a factory producing war material had this to say to him. This man's job was boring holes in pieces of iron. The foreman of the factory said, "We want you to drill fifteen holes to-day". The man replied, "Why, I can drill thirty." The manager said, "We are not asking you what you can do. We are telling you to drill fifteen." The man answered, "All right; I will drill two if you say so." This is the sort of thing that should be looked into by this committee, I contend, and this is exactly what I want to point out to the Prime Minister. I do not think the Minister of Munitions and Supply has time to investigate all these cases, but when members of this house have information such as this, I believe the committee should conduct a thorough investigation. Another man in the same factory, whose job was sawing metal, told me that the foreman said to him, "When anyone comes by, pretend you are cutting this piece of steel in two." Imagine that; he was to pretend he was doing some work!
We know that in the past delegations of workmen have come to Ottawa to interview various ministers. These skilled mechanics have come here from factories producing army trucks, and so on. They did not come to ask for any increase in wages; they came to complain because the factory was deliberately slowing down its .production. I do not need to tell hon. members what plants I have in mind; they know. These are perhaps the three largest plants in Canada. If the cabinet have not already interviewed another of these committees, they soon will be meeting a group of men who are coming down to see them in regard to paper production in Canada. I was astonished to hear, as I think the Prime Minister will be astonished when he hears, that although those in charge of the salvage campaign are advertising far and wide that there is a great shortage of paper and that we must save every scrap of paper we can, there is one large paper mill in this country which, in war time, is working only three days a week.

I do not think that is generally true, and I can give examples to the contrary.
I am not going to permit the hon. gentleman to interrupt like that.

I want to ask you this, Mr. Speaker. Is it true in one instance? If it is, that is a crime. Mr. Chairman, I should like-

Who is making this speech? I should like the hon. member to rise in his place and tell what he knows about the war effort-or possibly tell what he does not know about it. I am not concerned about that.

The Canadian National Railways president told us this afternoon that he could not get steel.

That is a different subject which we will bring up later on. We have a little information in regard to that, too.
I have had the pleasure, too, of visiting different kinds of war factories. I have not visited one aircraft factory yet that has not told me that with a very small amount of change and without any great expense involved they could almost double their production in planes. That is supposed to be one of the most important things we need. They told me that certainly there would have to be a little expansion. But for us to sit here idly by, when the next six months may see either success or defeat in this war, and sit as members of parliament knowing that these manufacturers are deliberately held back by the government-well, I think that is a shame, and I think it is time the Prime Minister knew it.
Mr. MACKENZIE* KING: May I say to my hon. friend that if manufacturers say they are deliberately held back by the government, they are saying something which they know nothing whatsoever about-less even than what my hon. friend knows. Hear, hear.

Go ahead and clap! Clap this one off: I had the president of the Ottawa Car and Aircraft in this city tell me that he was working on planes for which he did not have a government contract, and he said, "The only reason why I don't shut down is that we are in hopes that the government will accept it. But we cannot wait on the government; they are too slow."

He is taking
everything that is being said to him as gospel truth. But my hon.
friend is casting reflections on the government, on the war effort and on industry, and he is seeking to support his reflections by hearsay evidence.

The Prime Minister should withdraw that statement, because I made a reference before in the house to these 500 men being laid off in the Ottawa Car and Aircraft, and made it to the Department of Labour. What did they do? They did not know about it. I asked a question on the order paper as to how many war industries were working twenty-four hours a day, seven days a week, 365 days of the year, and the department did not know. Then I asked how many were working only part time, and they did not even know that. So I say that is a commencing point from which the Prime Minister could start his investigation. How are we going to know whether we are making an all-out war effort or not? That is a proper function of the house committee.
I have a further suggestion to make, that the scope of this committee should be extended to include purchasing and production. My only desire is to see that every man we can put to work is out there working, and that every factory in this country is working 365 days in the year. My only wish is to see that the work is proceeding. Let them have things right at their finger-tips to go ahead, and let them do as much expanding as they would like to do. The statement made by the Prime Minister in the house that everything physically possible would be made financially possible-I believe that was the expression-had not, I think, much effect. I do not think that has been followed out.
One of the great fears under which this government is working, probably one of their own making, is that'industry or big business has prevailed upon the government to such an extent that it has had to caution manufacturers that if we extend our war effort too greatly we are going to have too great a production, that we shall be making propeller shafts we cannot use, that we shall be making army trucks we cannot get rid of, and that we shall have too many things we shall not be able to use. It has a fear of what is going to happen after the war, instead of doing everything it possibly can to increase our war effort so that we shall be sure to win the war.
I am convinced that that is what is holding us back, or that that is one of the major factors. I believe one of the other factors to which reference has often been made in the house is the oil and gasoline supply. We are given to understand that we require oil and gasoline, and that this war might be lost for want of oil. Here again I direct my observations to the Department of Munitions and Supply. I do not believe the Minister of Munitions and Supply has time to look into all these things; but I do believe he has taken his advisers from the wrong sources.
I have some information in connection with the production of oil. I do not wish to go into too much detail, but my information-and incidentally I got it from the department- is that one of the reasons why the Alberta tar sands are not being developed is that the government believes it is not practicable at this time. So far as I can find out the only source from which the government has got its information is the heads of the big oil business, men who are either directly or indirectly financially controlling or interested in the production of oil in this country. My information is that it is a definitely established and proven fact that we can get oil and gasoline out of these tar sands and sell them on the commercial market to compete with the big oil companies, and that the by-products obtained

will more than pay for the manufacture of the gasoline. I have that from what I believe is a reliable source, from men who are interested in the oil business. They have never been able to make any headway with the government. I think there should be an investigation of this. I am quite convinced that Imperial Oil are not going to expand our oil industry unless they are forced to do so, or unless some other steps are taken to expand this industry. Let me bring up another matter in this regard. Mention has been made about carburettors and other inventions, I believe by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell). In fact it came out in the press that this carburettor had been put on a car and an actual demonstration made with witnesses present.
Do not believe everything you read in the papers.

The minister should not believe everything he reads in the papers. He is a member of the government and he should see that these things are investigated. I should like to ask the minister, through you, Mr. Speaker: has the government ever made any investigation of this Pogue carburettor? The minister shakes his head. It is my opinion that the research bureau here in Ottawa does not even know that such a carburettor exists. I have gone a little further in my investigation; I know that it does exist.
The carburettor certainly could not run a car two hundred miles on a gallon of gas.
Why would that be?
I have heard a good deal about that.

If we are going to go into the science of this thing we might take an hour or two to debate it. I doubt the minister's remarks because I do not think he knows whether a gallon of gasoline can be made to run a ear two hundred miles.
I know there was no such carburettor ever made that could take a car two hundred miles on a gallon of gas.

I should like to know how the minister knows. Here is another instance where there should be a thorough investigation. The minister doubts that there is a carburettor made which, when put upon a car, will run that car two hundred miles on a gallon of gasoline.
I do not doubt at all; I know there is not.

The minister is so sure of this, but I doubt his w'isdom in this regard. I will put the minister on the safe side and say that if the car would go only one hundred miles on a gallon, half that distance, would it not be a matter worth investigating? If it would go only a quarter of that, just think what it would do for our present supply-it would double it. I say that if there is any possibility at all, it should be investigated.
Get hold of Mr. Pogue and ask him to send it to the inventions board which checks on these things. You will find out that there never was such a carburettor.

There is. If the minister does not know it, he should. We are in the midst of a war. The Minister of Munitions and Supply contradicted the Minister of National War Services because the former said in this house that the very carburettor about which we are talking was thoroughly investigated by a man in Winnipeg, and that this man in Winnipeg had spent 140,000 to see if it was any good.

It was a different
carburettor entirely.
Than the one you are speaking of?
The one you are speaking of now.
No; it is the same carburettor. The minister is trying to back out of his statement because the Minister of Munitions and Supply did make that statement in the house.
They were totally different carburettors.

Hon. members across the house have taken a tremendous amount of my time, and I hope, Mr. Speaker, you will be a little lenient with me until I finish. I shall not be much longer.

War Expenditures-Mr. Johnston (Bow River)
I regret to have to inform the hon. member that his time has elapsed.
That is fine. I will remember that even though it is a minister speaking.

Mr. Speaker, in spite of the argument about carburettors and the bickering back and forth across the floor of the chamber during the course of this debate, I for one have learned more about the workings and objectives of this committee than I knew before the debate commenced. I had not intended taking any part in the debate until the hon. member for Renfrew South (Mr. McCann), the hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis), the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) and the minister himself had spoken. I am not going to detain the committee at any length. The hon. member for Renfrew South, as reported on page 1992 of Hansard, said:
I laugh when I read the personnel of the committee, and I laugh at myself when I am put on the fisheries committee, when I do not know any more about lobsters or the fishing industry than other hon. gentlemen know about medicine.
I congratulate the hon. member for Renfrew South upon the contribution he has made to the debate. I hope that when the membership of committees is being considered, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and other leaders in the house will remember what the hon. member has said. I am one of those who believe that a member appointed to a committee should have some knowledge of the matters that may be brought before that committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext: It is a good way to acquire knowledge.

The four members from this side who have been appointed will, I believe, render excellent service on that committee. Two of them are manufacturers with large plants, and their long business experience in buying and selling, in organizing and building their plants should fit them to sit on a committee of this kind.

How about
the lawyers?

Another one has had long experience in dealing with labour and in business. The fourth is a well known barrister who has sat on the bench and who has had the experience of weighing and sifting facts. I am quite pleased with the members from this group who have been placed on this
committee. I have nothing to say about the other members of the committee; they are all good men, having a good deal of experience in many matters. Of the twenty-four, I believe fourteen are barristers; four are manufacturers, while the other four are farmers or closely associated with the soil in some way.
The hon. member for Renfrew South did not pass any comment on the members of the committee, nor do I. I agree with what he said, that the committee should be enlarged if it is to do better work. If that is to be done, I looked through the red book to see what hon. members could render excellent service on this committee. The hon. member for Eglinton (Mr. Hoblitzell), has had considerable experience, not only in business but in the erection of oil stations, buildings and so on for the distribution of oil.
He must have had a lot of experience that would be valuable to any committee set up to delve into contracts. The same thing applies to the hon. member for York East (Mr. McGregor), who is a contractor of some note over the whole province of Ontario. His experience ought to be of material assistance to a committee inquiring into contracts. The same thing applies to the hon. member for Prince Edward-Lennox (Mr. Tustin), who is a manufacturer, a dealer in lumber, a builder and contractor, and so forth. The hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand) is a business man with a lot of experience who would be valuable on the committee. Another hon. member who would be valuable on the committee is the senior member for Halifax (Mr. Isnor). I have observed him on committees and have always admired his keen ability to bore right into the centre of things. The hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Hatfield), is one of the big business men of the maritime provinces. Another valuable member on the committee would be the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Hill). The hon. member for Queens-Lunenburg (Mr. Kinley), who is not in his seat at the moment, is a man with whom I have had much conversation, and I am convinced that with his wide knowledge of business and manufacturing he looks at business from a practical point of view. The hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Lacroix), whom I see in his seat to-night, would be a valuable member of the committee. He has had much experience in matters pertaining to lumber, timber and business of that kind. Many lumber contracts will come before the committee, and he could give excellent assistance to the committee. The hon. member for Waterloo North (Mr. Breithaupt) has
