been associated for years with a large manufacturing business. I believe his family are one of the largest manufacturers in one line of business in Canada. I believe he would be an excellent choice for the committee. The hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Moore) *would be of great assistance to the committee. There is, in my judgment, no more able man in matters pertaining to business. The hon. member for Northumberland, Ontario, (Mr. Fraser) is another business man who is an employer of labour and operates large plants. The hon. member for Peterborough West (Mr. Fraser) has had a lot of experience in manufacturing. Who has had more experience in timber and lumber contracting than the hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Hanson)? Then there is the hon. member for Yale (Mr. Stirling), an able engineer. He would be an excellent member on such a committee. I do not believe that an engineer has been named to the committee. I am afraid I am leaving many out. The hon. member for Lincoln (Mr. Lockhart) is another prominent business man with a wide experience in contracting which would be valuable to the committee. The hon. member for Duf-ferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) is associated with one of the large paper businesses in Canada. While that line of business has not been much discussed in parliament lately, it was referred to by the hon. member who has just taken his seat (Mr. Johnston, Bow River). He would be a valuable member of the committee. Then men like the hon. member for Kent, Ontario, (Mr. Desmond), the hon. member for Huron North (Mr. Cardiff), the hon. member for Haldimand (Mr. Senn), are all farmers with wide experience in cattle raising and in the meat industry. All of the men I have mentioned, as well as many others I could name, would be of great assistance to the committee.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
What about the hon. member for Davenport (Mr. MacNicol) ? Has my hon. friend forgotten him?
Mr. MacNlCOL: Others have had more experience than I have had. Therefore, if the suggestion made by the hon. member for Renfrew South is to be considered and the membership widened, I suggest that some of those I have mentioned be appointed to the committee. It might also be necessary to appoint one or two more barristers who are trained to look into contracts, but I would not have a committee composed entirely of barristers. I would have a good number of practical men on the committee. I am not saying that barristers are not practical men, 
but they are not as practical as men who work in business and in industry, such as the hon. member for Danforth (Mr. Harris), the hon. member for Waterloo South (Mr. Homuth) and other members I have named. That is all I have to say about the personnel of the committee.
The Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson) this afternoon lauded the government plants. I am not going to say anything against them because I do not think that criticism of the government plants would help the war effort, and by criticism I mean denunciation of them. I suppose the government built its own plants, or had others build them, because manufacturers may not have wanted to assume the first cost of manufacturing special munitions of war without being compensated. But I disagree with the minister when he states that these plants are operating at 100 per cent efficient capacity in all cases. He may not have said that in so many words, but he gave that impression. I tell the minister that, in my opinion, no government plant can be operated 100 per cent efficiently, and that is not finding fault with the plant itself. It is merely because of the fact that it is the government that is operating the plant instead of a private individual or company. It is no reflection on the government, and so I hope the government will not take that as a criticism.
Let me give an example. My long experience in plants enables me on going through a plant to form my own judgment as to how the plant is being operated, whether it is being operated as I had to operate a plant.
I have been in different plants operated by the government where I have seen at times many men standing idle by their machines for some considerable time. It was not the men's fault because I have talked with these men and asked them why they were not working. They told me that their machines were not operating because the materials for their machines were not available or because the plant could not get the materials, and I presume that the government, being a benevolent employer, does not do what a private operator is compelled to do when there is no material available to keep a machine operating. There is only one thing the private operator can do in such a case, and that is to send the men home. But the government does not need to do that because it has all that is required, so far as finances are concerned, to operate the plant. Let me say right here that I am not in accord with sending men home simply because the material is not available for them to work with. It is not fair to the workmen, and I

War Expenditures-Mr. MacNicol
hope when this war is over and the whole setup pertaining to labour is reorganized, that men present and willing to work in the plant in -which they are engaged but not having the material to work with, will be compensated if they are laid off through no fault of their own. I think the time has gone by when the working man-and I was one for years-can be called back and forth at the will of the operator of the plant. It is not fair to the working man. It is not just. So perhaps, when the government or those who are operating these plants for the government, when they keep a man on, standing around doing nothing, are doing it because of humanitarian reasons. I look forward to the day when the working man will be treated throughout the whole of industry as he ought to be treated. But as I said, the minister was wrong, if unintentionally. He must know that a government-operated plant cannot function with the same degree of efficiency as a private institution properly managed.
The hon. member for Vancouver East said, if I remember it correctly, that not a single contract had been investigated since the committee was set up. The hon. member for Lake Centre asserted that the committee of which he was a member had not sat for more than thirty or forty hours altogether since it was constituted. If contracts are not to be investigated where necessary-I do not mean all contracts, for, as the minister well said, that would be impossible-the committee is not performing one of its most important duties. I do not suggest that the purpose of investigating a contract should be to unearth a scandal. I would be opposed to blazing before the public any scandal in connection with a government contract. Where the chairman or the minister has received evidence of something wrong, I would endorse an investigation in camera; first because, as the minister said, the publicizing to the country of scandals in time of war will not help the national effort; second, the purpose of such an investigation should not be to publish scandal but to encourage responsible authority to take the measures necessary to prevent a recurrence of what has been found wrong. There is a saying handed dow-i by the Great Teacher, "He that is without sin among you, let him first cast a stone." All my life I have been careful about casting stones against anybody. You can never tell how far they are going to roll.
They might rebound.

There are things which a committee could find out that might be rectified. I myself have made a number of investigations. Recently I inspected a building
which had been erected under the government's direction. I am not condemning the government on account of what contractors or the men under their direction do, nor am I relating this to show that there is anything wrong other than extravagance. The boards on the exterior of the framework were planed on both sides; tarpaper or some other kind of insulating paper was attached to the outside planed surface, and then another, better sheathing was put outside that. On the inside, of course, the scantlings were lathed and plastered. The building was a large one and required a great quantity of this kind of lumber. As I went through the place, examining it, I thought to myself, for what reason would many, perhaps hundreds of thousands of feet of lumber, which is covered on one side with scantling, lathed and plastered, and covered on the other side with paper, be planed on both sides? Lumbermen may say that it costs no more than rough lumber, but it does not seem to me that that can be so; surely lumber costs more planed than unplaned. This is not a crime, but it is an extravagance. In these times, when the minister by means of large paid advertisements is begging everybody to save every scrap of paper, every bit of brass, every piece of iron which can be saved, for what reason is such high-class lumber used only to be covered up?
Let me mention another ease. Perhaps the boiler part of the John Inglis plant is not under the government, but at any rate one section of the plant makes boilers and another part makes small arms. In a government building only a stone's throw from the John Inglis plant two boilers were installed which, if my memory serves me aright, came from a plant many miles away. Perhaps the John Inglis company did not have boilers on hand; but it struck me, after twenty-five years of keen business experience, as a most peculiar thing to transport boilers a thousand miles for installation in a building so close to a plant which is under government direction and which manufactures boilers.
One day I talked to a man who was trucking material from Hamilton. Its final destination was Niagara Falls, but first it was brought to Toronto and then it went to Camp Borden. I asked the man, "Why are you going to Camp Borden?" He said, "Oh, that is where it is to be inspected." So it was to be taken to Camp Borden, in Simcoe county, fifty miles or more from Toronto, then brought back to Toronto, then along the Hamilton highway to Niagara Falls, where the material was to be installed.
Perhaps such things as these cannot be avoided, but I believe if they were brought

War Expenditures*-Mr. MacNicol
before a committee examining into contracts they would represent only a few of very many instances where savings could be made. At this time everybody should exert the utmost possible effort to economize. The main purpose of this committee should be to bring about economy; if it does that, it will have done something worth while.
In the course of his address the minister, as I understood him, referred to the eighth report, which was in connection with medical work. At that time I said to myself, "I will check over the names of the committee to see if there is a doctor on it", and I did not find one. I assume that that fact is what inspired the very apt remarks of the hon. member for Renfrew South. In any event, how a committee composed of everyone but doctors can issue a medical report is more than I can understand. So I will say to the hon. member for Renfrew South that I agree that there should be a doctor on the committee. As the hon. member for Danforth said, the question of hospitals was considered by the committee, and on anything pertaining to hospitals of course the hon. member for Renfrew South or the hon. member for Wood Mountain (Mr. Donnelly) or any other medical * doctor in the House of Commons would be an excellent addition to the committee.
Last year on June 10, the hon. member for Danforth made some very constructive remarks. In some of them he went after the committee or the committee's report pretty hard, which led me to believe that the committee was a useless committee as I said this afternoon, but perhaps it was not as useless as the word would imply. The hon. member said, as reported on page 3764 of Hansard of June 10, 1941:
Let the private serving in the ranks know that we are helping. Let the contractor who wants to obtain a government contract know that we are not only helping him but also watching him, in order to see that the contract is fair and right.
That is good, sound doctrine; no one can object to that. The hon. member was not seeking scandal when he said that; he talked as a business man of many years' experience, for he has to operate his plant with the greatest care. He cannot afford to pay two prices for the material he buys, nor can he waste money; he has to run his plant in a business way, and that is why he made this statement:
Let the officers in our camps, who are looking after the men, know that we are anxious to help them, but that any extravagance on their part is going to be checked.
I hope that when the committee reconvenes, all matters such as the hon. member for

Danforth has mentioned will be subject to scrutiny by that committee; not to find scandals, far from it, but to effect economies, as the minister says is the purpose of the committee.
That, I think, covers all I have to say in connection with the committee. H the Prime Minister does follow the suggestion of the hon. member for Renfrew South, I hope he will nominate some of these able members that I mentioned or others I could have mentioned, who would bring to that committee a wealth of experience in handling contracts, in buying, in selling, in engineering, in various lines of big business, experience that would enable them to present to the government something constructive and to assist the government in carrying on this war activity as these men who are in business have to carry on their own businesses.

Mr. Speaker the preamble of
the resolution now under discussion reads as follows:
Resolved that a select committee be appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war, and to report what, if any, economies consistent with the execution of the policy decided by the government may be effected therein,
The committee of inquiry on war expenditures with which the house is now dealing should not, this time, be content with skimming the subject. The Canadian people, who are staggering under a heavy burden of taxes and who lend their savings to the government for the prosecution of war, have a right to know how the public moneys are spent. It is high time that light should be thrown upon these abuses that are so frequently pointed out to us.
I have condemned in parliament and on the hustings the wastefulness which has been discovered in the granting of contracts for foodstuffs by the government to some companies which have made profits of 18 to 20 cents per pound on the butter sold to military training camps. I have urged the government to curb the wanton greed of the same contractors, who are still delivering to the army, at prices varying from $2 to S2.50 a bag, potatoes that were put in storage at 50 and 60 cents a bag, at the beginning of last fall and winter. I have directed the attention of the Minister of Munitions and Supply upon the theft of foodstuffs intended for the soldiers at Valcartier. I ask the government, moreover, to conduct a searching inquiry upon the disappearance of 240 wool blankets

War Expenditures-Mr. Lacombe
out of 5,000 delivered to military district No. 5 by a manufacturer of Cap St. Ignace. The Canadian people, as well as parliament, have the right and the duty to track down at all times and everywhere those who are guilty of dishonesty. Is it true that there was a shortage of coal at the Petawawa military camp last winter, while the temperature was 20 or 30 degrees below zero?
If this is so, what are the causes of this shortage and who is responsible for it? The proposed investigation should bear on all irregularities and abuses which, rumour has it, are occurring in our war plants. It is the government's inescapable duty to investigate the wastage of materials and man-power which certain persons, employed in these industries as foremen or labourers, unceasingly report to us. It is high time parliament reassumed control over public expenditures. The bureaucracy and the civil service have everywhere replaced the representatives of the people, and responsible government is about to expire in the hands of a man, who, in 1926, showered Lord Byng of Yimy with the thunderbolts of government responsible to the people. "The king reigns but does not govern," he cried at the time. Who is governing to-day? A gang of bureaucrats who ceaslessly trample underfoot the privileges of the elected representatives of the people. Who is governing to-day? Boards established by order in council without consulting parliament. Who is governing to-day? The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, the most pernicious instrument of election propaganda ever known. Who is governing to-day? The Wartime Prices and Trade Board, where flourishes already the most cynical favouritism toward trusts and companies in the very good graces of the administration. Who is governing to-day? Shady contractors dealing with the department of munitions and supply, who pay the cost of monstrous advertisements for the purpose of eliciting a "Yes" vote from the people at the plebiscite. Who is governing to-day? The trusts, friendly to the government, who, under the minister of revenue's signature, were already abusing those who would vote "No" on plebiscite day, comparing them to Hitler.
Mr. Speaker, never, in the course of the last century, has our country assumed a more colonial status in the hands of this oligarchy which threatens to make short-work of provincial autonomy, of our constitution, our laws, our agriculture, our industries, our commerce, our man power, our youth and all the living strength of the nation.
How deplorable is the ignorance of dishonesty of the bureaucracy who recently froze
the price of maple syrup at last year's level, without considering the cost of labour which has increased threefold. This is not all. The public accounts committee, who seem to be nothing but a name, should hold meetings as soon as possible. This committee should be empowered to scrutinize all war contracts and first those awarded to the government's pets, Messrs. J. A. A. Leclair and J. H. Dupuis, the first being the chief organizer of the Quebec provincial Liberal machine. Here are the values of the contracts awarded to Messrs. J. A. A. Leclair and Dupuis: $29,591.63, $34,684.13, $7,793.64, $27,700; and the amounts already paid to the same contractors, Mr. Speaker, are as follows: $29,591.63, $34,684.13, $7,792.64.
After this contractor is paid a further amount of $27,500, he will have received approximately $100,000. In view of the peculiar position of J. A. A. Leclair in the Liberal party set-up, it is essential that we have all details and correspondence regarding these contracts.
As to the provincial member for Laval, Mr. Frangois Leduc, civil engineer, this foremost promoter of an affirmative answer to the plebiscite question, has received from the federal government, from September 7, 1940, to December 1, 1941, the sizeable amount of $14,379.69. What for? In payment for professional advice and inspection services in connection with the Bagotville and Mont Joli airports.
From now on, there will be no mystery as to why the provincial member for Laval seconded the amendment to the Chaloult motion at the Quebec legislature.
Let us now revert to the present administration's abuses. The Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, during the plebiscite campaign, which has cost millions of dollars to the country, have resorted to shameless discrimination. Who will pay for the broadcasting of the speeches delivered by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King), the cabinet members and the party leaders who supported him?

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order! The hon. member must resume his seat. I call the hon. member's attention to the fact that the motion before the house does not warrant a discussion of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation nor of government administrative orders. The matter submitted to the house is the expediency of forming a committee to investigate war expenditures. The hon. member may not review the various contracts awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply, as this will be the task



War Expenditures-Mr. Lacombe
of the committee. The matter submitted to the house is simply the advisability of forming' such a committee.

Mr. Speaker, submitting to your ruling, I now revert to the subject.
What a prodigal spirit seems to animate our governments. Never have expenditures been higher, never have so many gifts been made at the expense of our national economy. According to reliable information, our forest resources are being dissipated on the spot. Considerable quantities of wood, copper, steel and even oil and gasoline are being shamefully wasted in our war plants. When will these reprehensible abuses come to an end? Let the committee see to it and enquire into the smallest details.
Moreover, the R.C.M.P. should be authorized to search and keep an eye on registrars' offices throughout the country. We all know, Mr. Speaker, the disgusting transactions that have taken place in some of these offices. Exemptions have been sold to Rumanians, Syrians, and even to citizens hailing from countries now at war with us. I have often been told that favouritism, bought with gold, has covered up many other cases to the detriment of fairness and honesty, of the war effort and the defence of this country.
Lastly, there is another matter which the committee should not overlook, that is the expropriation of lands required for war industries, aerodromes, military camps, and so forth. Why should the 4,000 acres of land formerly belonging to Georges Vandelac, of . Montreal, and which he purchased from the Terrebonne county council for less than $200, for the taxes owing on the property, have been sold to the authorities for a price of $44,000?
I rise to a point of order.
That should prove to be a very interesting matter.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: Order! The hon. member for Sainte-Marie has risen to a point of order.

I believe that the hon.
member for Laval-Two Mountains, discussing in this house the advisability of forming an investigation committee, has no right to name certain persons and to bring against them charges of having obtained favours and money under false pretences. He named a moment ago Mr. Leclair, among others. I think-

Mr. Speaker, on this
point of order I would remind my hon. colleague for Sainte-Marie that he is out of

order. He is not entitled to make a speech aside from the point of order he has raised.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Are there any
members who wish to speak on the point of order? If not, I must once again bring to the attention of the hon. member who has the floor that he must not go into facts which will be examined later by the committee. I have already pointed out to the hon. member for Laval-Two Mountains, that it is not in order to cover details when one is speaking on the question of principle, on the advisability of forming a committee. I trust that the hon. member will heed this further warning.

Mr. Speaker, I shall conclude my remarks in a few moments. However, since the hon. member for Sainte-Marie, speaking on a point of order, has taken a hand in the debate, I wish to tell him without further ado that I have brought no charges against anyone. I merely pointed out to the house the amount of certain contracts awarded to certain people and I asked that they be scrutinized. That is all. I did not make a'ny charge. The committee will attend to that. It will be its duty to do so. The honourable member has not understood me; neither have the electors of St. Mary at the last election and still less on the occasion of the plebiscite.
That is why your candidate was defeated.
I believe the hon. member will be defeated by a majority of 22,000 at the next election and that he will swallow his pill once for all.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
I must direct
the attention of the hon. member to the matter that is now before the house. The plebiscite is not under discussion. The honourable member has no right to discuss it at this time.

Mr. Speaker, I do not
intend to discuss the plebiscite, but the holding of that plebiscite was ordered by the house on a matter closely connected with the war.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The matter is settled by the decision I have given. Will the hon. member now discuss the subject that is before the house?

Mr. Speaker, let the
committee which will sit shortly be relentless and adamant; let it summon all witnesses whose examination may be essential if the necessary evidence is to be obtained, and it will render a splendid service to the country and the Canadian ratepayers.

War Expenditures-Mr. Castleden

War Expenditures-Mr. Castleden
should like the Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) to give the house the assurance now that it will be the duty of this committee to investigate all expenditures. The resolution reads:
That a select committee he appointed to examine the expenditure defrayed out of moneys provided by parliament for the defence services, and for other services directly connected with the war.
There is a question of what interpretation may be placed upon the phrase "other services directly connected with the war". I suppose it is possible the committee may decide that it should not investigate wartime housing because that is not directly connected with the war. I maintain that it is connected witth the war, and very directly. All expenditures of money passed by parliament should be a matter of investigation by parliament, and a report should be handed down and discussed here. Otherwise this parliament is not doing its duty to the Canadian people.
The Canadian people want to know that when their money is being spent they are getting a dollar's value for every dollar expended. They should be given the assurance-and this is most important whether the government thinks it is or not-that when they are giving their sons and their brothers, their fathers and their husbands to die in this conflict, no person will be permitted to use this terrible crisis as an opportunity to fill his pockets with a lot of tax-free bonds.

Mr. Speaker, the making of steel is a gigantic enterprise. I am prompted to refer to this industry because of some statements which were made by the hon, member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston). His remarks showed that he was getting into pretty deep water when he attempted to discuss the manufacture of machines fabricated from iron and steel. Last year the amount of ore shipped from the head of the lakes was some 80,000,000 tons, and enormous shipments were made from Newfoundland to the steel Mills of Nova Scotia. The ore is brought down to the steel mills, which are generally located conveniently to coal.
The first process is in the blast furnace. These blast furnaces are constructed of a great variety of materials, and many other materials enter into the process of making pig-iron. The next development is the production of steel and steel alloys made with combinations of nickel, chromium, molybdenum and other things brought from various

parts of the world. The hon. member for Bow River referred to the plant at Calgary, and we are all proud to know that there is the beginning of a steel and iron industry in that city. This industry will make use of pig-iron produced in these great blast furnaces as well as scrap iron collected in that part of the country. We must, however, realize that the manufacture of special steels, such as are used in aeroplanes, is not possible in a small plant of that kind. Steel that is used for different purposes must possess different qualities, such as elasticity, elongation, resistance to fracture and so forth.
The making of aeroplanes is also a gigantic enterprise. Aeroplanes are not constructed of one material; their manufacture necessitates the use of textiles, rubber and many other things. The first operation in constructing an aeroplane is carried out in these wooden buildings here in Ottawa-the designing that is done on the draughting tables and so forth. The next step is the manufacture of gauges, dies, tools, et cetera. In order to assemble an aeroplane, the products of many industries must be brought together. These include propellers, precision instruments and the products of industries in all parts of the country. I am giving this picture to indicate, first, that it cannot be expected that a small industry like this one in the west, far removed from the great volume of business of the eastern plants, whose production is devoted almost wholly to structural steel, could produce the great varieties of iron and steel that are required in our war industries.
In the production of an aeroplane it cannot be expected that there will never be any shortage of parts or materials. It is a well known fact that as the process of manufacture goes on, certain parts will pile up, while others will be missing due to unforeseen causes. This is not the fault of the manufacturer or the assembler; these delays have arisen in plants perhaps one or two thousand miles away, and they may have been caused by the non-arrival of certain component parts or materials from distant parts of the world. One cannot speak lightly of or criticize a situation about which he knows very little and into which so many elements enter.
All this gives us some idea of the responsibilities that rest upon the shoulders of our Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) and of the wonderful work he has done in building up the organization we have here. It has been necessary for him to call in experts from every line of industry in order that he may have the best advice, so that

War Expenditures-Mr. Gladstone
the whole effort can. be coordinated with the least possible delay and bring forth the greatest efficiency.
During my seven years in parliament I have seldom taken a strong political attitude. I may be regarded as rather a poor politician in a sense. It is my desire rather, always to view the problems that come before us from a business point of view and to contribute something, if I may, from that point of view. I had an opportunity during the past year of serving on the war expenditures committee, and I for one see many very important results of its work over a few months. The object of the committee is to promote efficiency, to save money, and to correct conditions that hamper our war effort and hurt our people. I am sure that in some respects the work of the committee has contributed a great deal toward giving confidence to our people as to the necessity of the efforts being put forward. While errors have been discovered, there has been a willingness and a desire on the part of those affected to have them corrected.
The statement was made to-day that there is a widespread feeling that enormous sums of money were being wasted, or possibly the statement was to the effect that millionaires were being created. That is a totally inaccurate statement. I am sure the people are confident that no millionaires are being created in this war, and there is also the circumstance that if they are being or should be created, there will, at all events, be no reward in the form of titles after this war is over.
There are many things for which the committee might well be praised, but it would not serve any useful purpose. I think it would be much better if I were to mention some ways in which we might improve our methods for the future, and this I shall endeavour to do briefly. Possibly I may be taken as criticizing the government's effort; but the function of this committee, I believe, is to act as a non-political group, looking to the promotion of efficiency and the saving of money in our war effort. I believe the attitude of the public so far has been that there has been justification for the committee, and that through the experience already gained there will be further opportunity for making corrections and promoting efficiency. If there has been any weakness or any handicap at all, I think it has been due to political psychology, a sort of feeling, perhaps, that the Liberals may mistrust the Conservatives and the Conservatives the Liberals, and even some of the other parties may be involved, for I think it may be said that they, too, are
rapidly acquiring some of those qualities or attitudes of the older parties which come under public criticism most frequently. So I would say, Mr. Speaker, that for the greater effectiveness of this committee we should endeavour to get rid in every possible way of this bone of contention that the committee may be desiring or is endeavouring to serve some political purpose to cover up certain situations. From my experience I would say that that is far from the truth.
This attitude of political fear seems to be closely associated with the question of open or closed meetings. There are advantages in some respects in closed meetings, and at other times there are advantages in open meetings. As has been stated, open meetings discourage at times the giving of evidence freely, and they may also foster the political viewpoint. Consequently, in an open meeting a member often makes a statement which gets a headline in the press; in using the head-line the press will refer to the speaker as a member of a certain political party, and so the press report itself gives a tinge of politics to the work of the war expenditures committee. It is inevitable that the press at open meetings should attempt to give publicity to the proceedings of the committee. That factor is eliminated in closed meetings. If we could have the assurance that political considerations were entirely eliminated by all parties represented on the committee, then I think the suggestion that has been made by some members of the opposition, that the membership of the committee be increased, could very well be regarded as having some merit. I believe that additional members of the opposition groups could contribute to the work of the committee.
One hon. member has referred to the fact that only eighty-three sittings were held during the year, taking up some 280 hours. That to a large extent is due to procedure and red tape. It is my feeling that even though the war expenditures committee is a committee organized to promote economy and efficiency, its own procedure in some respects was not of the best. Much waiting resulted from the fact that every word of evidence had to be taken down. I do not believe such a thing would be countenanced by a board of directors discussing a large business undertaking, and without this necessity of taking down every spoken word there [DOT]would have been the opportunity of holding a great many more meetings than were held. It is, I think, a weakness of the committee that we have had too much of this documentary procedure. There has been a great deal of interviewing witnesses beforehand, of

War Expenditures-Mr. Gladstone
which procedure one can hardly see the ifecessity; this, in turn, has imposed much work on the chairman of the committee. It seems to me that his work should be lightened by a wider distribution of the work among the members of the committee.
I believe that in some respects we were overstaffed, and that the money provided for the carrying on of the committee was expended too quickly. This caused postponements and adjournments and shortened the time that the committee operated. As a war expenditures committee we might set an example of economy, and in that respect we certainly were open to criticism.
The estimate provided for the committee contemplated the possibility of continued sittings during the adjournment of parliament. It seems to me that this committee should sit almost every week -while parliament is in recess, and that in the estimates a generous sum should be provided so that the committee should not be under the necessity of adjourning through lack of funds. I am sure that every economy will be exercised, but the committee ought not to be handicapped in this direction.
A good start has been made; much experience has been gained, and I am sure that, realizing some of the imperfections of the past, we shall be able to expedite the work and get more direct results which will be well worth while. We ought to replace to some extent the rigid system of public administration by the more direct methods employed in any well-ordered business. Let us develop a new pattern of approach, using new methods, enliminating red tape, of which we had some, and adopting a procedure whereby we shall get at the kernel of the matters before us with the least possible expense.
I believe there is a great purpose to be served by this committee. Generous provision should be made so that, in whatever numbers are decided upon, the committee may sit continuously until we have a new parliament; and I trust that we shall rid ourselves of any thought of suspecting one another of playing for political advantage, and get down to the real work of correcting situations which are not right, and of assisting the government and the great organization associated with our enterprise, so that we may put forth the greatest possible effort on the part of Canada in the struggle in which we are engaged.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. L. RALSTON (Minister of National Defence):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I desire to take about five minutes to put on record the facts -with regard to three or four points which were mentioned by the hon. member for Lake

Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker) with respect to recommendations of the committee affecting the administration of the elementary flying training and air observer schools.
The hon. member indicated that the house had not yet been told whether these recommendations had been implemented. I think he was unduly critical in that respect, because obviously my colleague the Minister of National Defence for Air (Mr. Power) will be here in connection with the resolution which is now before the house and will be giving a statement on matters which came up in connection with that committee, as those questions are raised. I do not believe there has been any opportunity yet for the army, the navy, the air or other departments affected formally to make a report to the house as to whether the recommendations have been put into effect. I want to say, speaking for the air force, the army and, I am sure, the navy as well, that reports have been prepared by these services to be presented to the committee in order to indicate the extent to which the recommendations in the report which was presented in November have been carried out.
Since, however, my hon. friend has mentioned two or three points and has indicated that we do not know whether they have been carried out, I should like to give the house this information.
In the first place my hon. friend said-I do not know where he got the information-that elementary schools are not conducted on a civilian basis in the old country.
Not to-day, was the evidence which was given.

Whether that evidence was given or not, the information I have is that some of the schools in England which were run on a civilian basis were turned to a service basis for a short time, but they are being turned back now and put on a civilian basis; and many of them were never changed.
I want to say also to my hon. friend-and I think he knows, although he did not mention the United States-that in the United States elementary schools are run by civilians. And by the way I do not see in the report of the committee any recommendation that the schools be changed from a civilian basis to a service one.
Far from it.
When was that done?
I cannot tell my hon. friend the exact date, but it was done some months ago, I am advised by the controller, Mr. Apedaile-
Is that a net profit?

It is the profit which is referred to in the report of the committee, and the committee recommended that the profit be changed from 50 to 25 cents per flying hour.
Another recommendation was made that the training contracts with elementary flying training schools should be further amended to provide that all profits of the schools should be invested in non-interest bearing Dominion of Canada bonds; and that recommendation has been implemented.
Next, there was the recommendation referred to by the hon. member for Lake Centre that all contracts with air observer schools, which are also operated by civilians, should be amended to reduce flying hour profits by 65 per cent, that is to say, from $1 to 35 cents. That recommendation was implemented, and the reduction was antedated to June 1, 1941.
Another point which my hon. friend mentioned was a suggestion that the stock of the companies should be held in trust for the elementary flying training clubs. The committee recommended a change in the dominion Companies Act whereby it would be provided that no private individual would receive anything by way of profits in the shape of dividends or distribution of assets. The proposal was that all the companies should have a uniform charter. I am advised that that matter has been fully gone into and that investigation of the matter discloses that a form of charter can be granted to the flying clubs under part 2 of the Companies Act without requiring amendment of the act except that the disposal of any residue of funds after winding up is not specially provided for. That is not considered a serious matter, because it is considered that no flying club would wind up except for lack of funds to carry on, and the matter is now under active consideration by the Department of the Secretary of State, the Canadian flying clubs' association and the deputy minister for air. I am told that the matter of uniform charters is practically completed, and that will be carried out.
Those are the four points mentioned by my hon. friend. I want to mention one other
thing that came out in the debate to-night. The hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston) dealt at some length with a device called the Pogue carburettor. I recognize the name because I had some correspondence about it some time ago. The hon. member rather insistently intimated that the government had paid no attention to the Pogue carburettor and that it was a revolutionary device which would save a tremendous amount of gasoline.
Last fall the master-general of the ordnance, having had the device brought to his attention -of course in that branch they have a great many load-carrying as well as fighting vehicles, and we are just as anxious as anyone to save gasoline-brought in Mr. Pogue. He was put on an allowance of $10 a day for six weeks. We provided in the department Doctor King, a mechanical engineer of the national research council who is a special expert on carburettors. They went out to the proving grounds, and for six weeks worked there with Captain Irvine, a highly trained technical man on dynamometers, by putting the carburettor itself to practical test on motor vehicles. That test was conducted for six weeks. I am sorry to say that from the point of view of practical application of the carburettor and the saving of gasoline, the test did not prove it a success. Mr. Pogue, I think, would be as ready to admit that as anyone. As a matter of fact, I think he saw what the defects were. I do not profess to be able to discuss the thing scientifically, but I can say that he gets increased mileage with his carburettor at a sacrifice of power or of speed. That is to say, if you do not have to have much power or go at slow speed, you can get a larger mileage, but if you have to increase the speed of the vehicle or require power for a full load, the mileage per gallon goes down or, to put it the other way, the gasoline consumption goes up. Therefore, with load-carrying vehicles, it proved quite impracticable because they have to have the full pull all the time, and it was impossible to get his carburettor attachment to work under those circumstances. Mr. Pogue has never been able to give the branch a carburettor which works without being constantly adjusted. I mean that literally; you have to get out from time to time on the road and adjust the carburettor, which, of course, makes it absolutely impracticable.
Mr. Pogue went home. He was told by Major James with whom he was in contact, that we were ready at any time to consider any improvements he could make. He has been working on his carburettor ever since. In fact I think he is in town at the present
War Expenditures-Mr. Howe

time. I know Major James arranged for him to get into B class in regard to gasoline rationing so that he could have an opportunity of developing his carburettor.
I have an idea that my hon. friend must have known something about that, and I cannot understand his attitude when he suggests that the government has paid no attention to this matter. Mr. Pogue has had the fullest opportunity of demonstrating his device. That opportunity is open to him now. All the help that the department can give is there for him and he knows it. He has been the first to express appreciation for the way in which the department has treated him. He said that the help he received was far more than he expected.
I do not know whether the minister iwas referring to me when he said I knew it, or whether he meant Mr. Pogue.
I said I assumed my hon. friend knew it.
I have had correspondence with Mr. Pogue. My information is they are still working on it, but not with the government.

I have stated that the government worked with him for six weeks; he comes to see Major James from time to time now, to report on the progress he is making in trying to find something which will do the work that has to be done, and Major James has cooperated with him to the extent that long after he ceased to work with the department, Major James arranged for him to get special gasoline privileges in order that he might continue his experiments.
It is still being conducted, is it?

speakeroldname: Hon. C. D. HOWE (Minister of Munitions and Supply):
speechtext:
In the course of this debate much has been said about the duty of the war expenditures committee to investigate the Department of Munitions and Supply. I think anyone who followed this debate would assume that up to this time someone had prevented this committee from investigating the Department of Munitions and Supply. Let me say that that department was the first department of government investigated by the committee. My officers were before the committee for, I think, some two weeks, were excused, and fully expected to be called back. We were visited by a man who said he was chairman of a subcommittee of the main committee to investigate the Department of Munitions and Supply. We gave him the information for
(Mr. Ralston.]
which he asked. I had a special officer delegated to see that the committee was served in any way that was required. It was the duty of this man to meet any members of the committee and to see that officers having special knowledge of the problems were placed at the disposal of the committee when required.
We have heard in the course of this debate many loose statements about the Department of Munitions and Supply, many from members of the committee. I suggest that the members of the committee are criticizing themselves when they make loose statements about the Department of Munitions and Supply. Here was a committee charged by parliament to investigate war expenditures, and now members of the committee rise in their places in this house and criticize the transactions of the department without ever having given the department a chance to lay the facts before them. I think it ill becomes any member of the committee, which has had all the facilities of the department placed at its disposal, to criticize the transactions of the department.
We have heard suggestions that there are men in plants who are not working as hard as they could work, and that there are plants which do not have all they could do. Surely it is the duty of the members of the committee to look into any case of that kind, obtain information on it and bring down a judicial finding, not just to make loose statements in this house. I believe two hon. gentlemen opposite visited my city and made a statement that they knew of thirty men who were out of work. I suppose thirty out of about 750,000 is a serious matter and worthy of comment. I am not objecting to statements of that kind, but I do say that when the information is readily available to members of the committee, such statements should not be made. It is very damaging to the war effort to have distrust built up about the Department of Munitions and Supply. I think the public in general have confidence that my department is carrying on its work honestly and with some efficiency. That being so, it is extremely important, when we are asking every man, woman and child in this country to buy war bonds, that that confidence should be preserved. If there is anything wrong with my department, there is no one more anxious to know about it than I am. We have special men constantly on the watch for irregularities or wrongdoing. We brought two or three men before the courts; they were brought before the courts, not by any outside investigators but by our own internal investigators. We shall be delighted if someone from the outside will give us a hand in finding any irregularities that may exist. I can assure hon. members

War Expenditures-Mr. Marshall
that if there has been any irregularity, the guilty party will be punished to the full extent that the courts provide punishment.
I do not know that I should go into the specific charges that have been made in rather a loose way, whether or not it is worth dealing with them. I do say, however, that during this debate I have heard nothing which I am not prepared to discuss fully with the committee at any time. The files in my department are open to the committee. By international agreement we have undertaken not to publish lists of contracts, or to make public certain information. Those rules are much stricter to-day than they were a few months ago; but as far as the committee is concerned, and as long as it meets in camera, we are prepared to lay any document in the department before it or to have any of our officers appear before it to discuss any situation the members might wish to discuss.
I felt that I should say this. I believe every member of, this house knows that what I have said is the situation, but just to keep the record straight I thought a statement of this kind on my part was warranted.

Mr. Speaker, I was honoured by my group by being appointed to the committee set up last session to investigate war expenditures. I regret that circumstances over which I had no control did not permit me to attend all the sessions that were held, but I wish to say that my relations with the other members of the committee were of the most cordial nature. I looked upon the work of the committee not in any partisan or political light but rather as a service I might give my country, because of my inability to serve in any other capacity. I gave up my work on the committee quite willingly, and for the balance of the time this group was represented by the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) who, I believe, carried on in a very creditable manner. I feel sure that the hon. member who will represent us this year, the hon. member for Bow River (Mr. Johnston), will bring to the work of the war expenditures committee the same high purpose and high motives which inspired those who performed this work last year.
I listened with strict attention to the remarks of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), and as a private member I desire to say that I agree with the minister in almost every particular. I fully realized from the beginning that we were not engaged simply in a fishing expedition. Rather our object was, as the minister stated,
to view the situation in the broadest possible way and bring to the government and to the officials of the department helpful recommendations. I did not delude myself into thinking that this was a one-year job or a two-year job. It is a job that will tax the ingenuity of the members of the committee during the entire period of this war.
As a member of the war expenditures committee I understood that there was a definite and clear distinction between its work and that of the public accounts committee. I understood, further, that if anything came to our attention which seemed irregular, we could pass the information along to the public accounts committee for investigation. We spent a number of the early sessions in becoming thoroughly conversant with the routine operations of the Department of Munitions and Supply. This, to me at least, was fundamentally essential to the work which was to follow. If I were to offer any criticism in regard to the work done during the time I was a member of the committee, I should say that our meetings were too infrequent. We should have met more often in order to clear away the preliminary work with dispatch, and get down to matters of greater consequence.
I desire now to say a word or two about sittings in camera. As I understood it, there was more or less unanimity among the members of the committee with respect to this question. It was understood and agreed that we should sit in open session most of the time, but that if any matters came up of such a nature as to warrant a session in camera, the general committee or the subcommittee would weigh the facts and, if they were found to be sufficiently significant, would readily agree to such a sitting. But after many years of working on committees of various kinds I have come to the conclusion that sittings in camera are a joke. They are made such by the members themselves, who do not appear to know the meaning of the term "in camera" or the words "on your honour." I will admit that a very large amount of information which was given to us in the various sittings which were held in camera was of such a commonplace nature that it could have been given quite properly in an open session. One of the most informative articles I have ever read was published in Maclean's Magazine, and the information which formed the basis of that article was given in camera in a session of the committee of this house. I discovered that information of a more or less confidential nature was being constantly given out with perfect freedom and with utter abandon; and for that reason I believe the sittings in camera are a joke.



War Expenditures-Mr. Marshall
There seems to be some confusion, in the minds of some hon. members about the war expenditures and the public accounts committees. It has been stated that the war expenditures committee has superseded the public accounts committee. If that is actually the situation, then I deplore it. I believe a very important part can be played by both the war expenditures committee and the public accounts committee.
As a member of the public accounts committee I frankly confess I have been disappointed because it has not been functioning. It should function, not for the purpose of washing dirty linen or of endeavouring to make political capital out of some situation, but rather to run down some of these insinuations, accusations, rumours and allegations which crop up from time to time. Let me cite an example. On one occasion I heard a member of the house make the statement that a building which normally would cost a million dollars would eventually cost two million. The information was given in such a way as to lead one to believe that something was radically wrong. I recall that the Minister of Munitions and Supply said he would see that a matter of this sort would be thoroughly investigated, and that an individual making an allegation such as that would be compelled to substantiate his statement. I have waited a long, long time, but nothing has come of that.

As a member of the committee may I ask the hon. member why, if he considered that situation serious, he did not investigate it at first hand, and call for documents. I cannot be expected to run down every rumour.

We were told definitely by the chairman of the war expenditures committee that matters of that sort did not fall within the purview of the committee, but rather were a question for the public accounts committee. It should not be necessary for any individual to rise in his place and make direct accusations in order to bring the public accounts committee together. The simple fact that a statement has been made should be the basis upon which we would be called together to run down an allegation, and see what it was all about.
I believe most of the recommendations made by the war expenditures committee would have been put into effect eventually, even if they had never been recommended by that committee. They were too obvious to be overlooked by a first-class business executive. I claim that nothing has been done thus far by the war expenditures committee which could not have been done in

less time, at less expense and with less fuss by one good civilian cost accountant, one good office management expert and an experienced businessman. A committee of three men of this calibre would have accomplished more in one month than the war expenditures committee accomplished in the whole year.
However, the ground work has been laid, and the committee can build from that ground work. If irregularities can be found, I suggest that they be referred to the public accounts committee. I believe we who constitute the membership of that committee will endeavour to find out the real saboteurs of Canada's war effort, and recommend to the house what treatment should be meted out to them.
Canada is fighting for her national existence, and has given the "full speed ahead" signal to her Prime Minister. I assure the Prime Minister that I for one stand ready to do my part to see that we win this war, and to see, too, that proper punishment is meted out to those human vultures who would feed on the lives of patriotic Canadians.

I am going to be brief and explicit in what I have to say. I am prompted to rise at this time by the remarks of the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson), who was chairman last year of the war expenditures committee. According to what he said, the committee did not have a very clear conception of its duties. In defending the activities of the committee this afternoon he made the statement that the probing into war contracts let by the Minister of Munitions and Supply (Mr. Howe) was not the function of the committee, that it was not a fact-finding committee.

I did not say it was not
the function of the committee; I said it was not the primary function.
That is only quarrelling with words.
There is a big difference.

The Minister of Munitions
and Supply now tells us that the vouchers and records of his department were open to the committee at any time they wanted to make an examination. I consider the work of the war expenditures committee to be one of the most important functions of this parliament.
I believe one of the best ways of maintaining the morale of the Canadian people at the present time is to guarantee that the money appropriated by means of war taxation is being spent to the greatest advantage in Canada's war effort. In going through certain sections of the country from time to time I find

War Expenditures-Mr. Gillis
serious misgivings on the part of the people as to whether this is being done. In my opinion the committee should have been functioning since the outbreak of the war. It has a task of great magnitude before it; it will have to go back into the business which has been transacted since the outbreak of the war. A statement by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. MacKinnon) which appeared in the Monetary Times of January 10, 1942, gives a clear picture of what the committee is up against at the present time. Referring to the war effort generally and war expenditures, he said:
Its efforts in this direction are being stimulated by the war contracts awarded by the Department of Munitions and Supply, which at the end of September had reached the enormous total of approximately $2,600,000,000. In order that our industries may be able to carry out their contracts, some $550,000,000 has been provided in the form of capital assistance for the construction of new plants, the extension of old plants, and the installation of new machinery and equipment. Again, since shipping is required to win the battle of the Atlantic and to carry our products to overseas markets, a programme of some $500,000,000 of new shipping has been authorized and some of these ships have already been launched. Indeed, our shipbuilding industry employs eight and nine times as many workers as it employed at the outbreak of war.
The wages of most of these workers have been frozen. From time to time the general public get the picture from the press that the workers in Canada consider that they are not getting what they should get in the way of wages and working conditions. They believe that production is not what it should be as exemplified in the steel industry, the mining industry and the shipbuilding industry. Union men have set up, of their own volition, production committees to see if industry cannot be speeded up. They are not quarel-ling about the question of wages.
The war expenditures committee is the only guarantee that the Canadian public have that the money is being spent to the greatest advantage. As I see it, the committee has avoided inquiry into the expenditures made by the different departments. According to the report which the committee made last year, I consider that its work was wasted. It inquired into the headquarters set-up of national defence, air, navy and army. There was no necessity for that. The different ministers come before the house with appropriations for their respective departments and we can make our inquiries from them. There is no necessity of a committee sitting in camera to inquire into the normal or natural expenditures of these departments. What is needed is an inquiry into the enormous expenditures made by way of contracts let,
44561-130}
not only by the Department of Munitions and Supply but by the Department of National Defence. There is a great necessity to dispel the rumours that are being circulated. As an example, I would mention the airport at Sydney, Nova Scotia, a national defence project. People whom I consider as responsible have asked me questions about this. One of the tenders for the original contract for the construction of the buildings at this airport was $250,000, but it was refused. Yet the buildings were finally completed at a cost of $1,500,000. Why was this tender not accepted? This is the rumour, and I do not know whether it is true or not.
May I suggest to the hon. member that he should not help to spread rumours of that kind. As a member of the committee he could get the facts.
I am not a member of the committee.

Surely the hon. gentleman
has friends. They only need to meet tomorrow and ask for vouchers on that, and the documents will be right there and every question will be answered.
The committee has not met since August.
I suppose it will meet when this debate ends. As far as I can see, my hon. friend is preventing it from meeting.
We have not prevented it from meeting during the last three months.

If the war expenditures committee were functioning as it should be, I could answer these rumours by saying that that was not possible, that there was a stop-block in the war expenditures committee which was checking these things. But the committee has not been fulfilling this function.
I suggest that the hon. member's criticism should be of the committee and not of the way in which contracts are let.
It should be of the government for not setting up the committee sooner.

speakerposition: Minister of Pensions and National Health
speechtext:
It was not our fault.
Mr. COLDWELiL: It was not our fault because we nominated our men early in the session.

That is not the only rumour I have heard. The hon. members for Halifax might have heard this one. The exhibition buildings in Halifax were taken over by the navy and were occupied" for a short time.
War Expenditures-Mr. Oillis

When they moved in, the 'building was completely equipped with new plumbing. Then the army took over, and all the heating and radiation equipment and the plumbing was taken out and a new set-up put in. That should be investigated.

I am here waiting to go on with the details of the appropriations for my department. That is a question my hon. friend could ask me to-morrow or to-night if we finish this debate. He does not need a committee to do that.

The war expenditures committee should have been functioning since the outbreak of the war and then these rumours would not be circulating. We would have the machinery provided to stop such matters, or to investigate them. As I said before, it will not be possible to check current matters for some time because the committee is going to go back over the war expenditures of the last two or three years. This afternoon the Minister of National War Services, the chairman of the committee, pointed out that there was some misconception about the duties of the committee. It certainly did not perform the functions I thought it was set up to perform.
Another matter that should be checked is the ability of those who receive contracts to carry them out. Most of the criticism I have heard along this line is with respect to contracts let by the Department of National Defence. When a firm of undertakers is given the contract to construct buildings, put in runways and so forth on an air field, it certainly does not look good. The opinion among many people whom I have met is that it is simply pouring money down the sink. As the minister said a moment ago, the workers are being asked to buy war savings certificates, and they are doing it. They are doing their best to win the war. But the general opinion is that it is a partisan war, so far as the government is concerned, in the letting of contracts, and the committee can perform a useful and constructive service to the country if it will get down to business and make an examination of the many criticisms that are being levelled at the government on that score. I do not know whether it is true or not; I should like to know; it is the duty of the committee to find out.
Many members of the committee have stated in the house that the committee could not do this or could not do that. I think it is the duty of any member of the committee, if he is not satisfied with how the majority of the committee are handling its business and filing its reports, to come before this house with a minority report and let us know just what the trouble is.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Secretary of State for External Affairs; President of the Privy Council
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think the best service it is possible for me to render to the committee and to the country in this matter is to make as brief a speech as possible and let the committee get on with its work immediately. There is little to be added from the government benches to what has already been said by my colleague, the Minister of National War Services (Mr. Thorson). In his address this afternoon the minister reviewed very comprehensively the work of the committee, and what had been accomplished by way of organization and investigation. I think he left the impression on the house, which indeed has been left generally by those who have spoken, that there is now a distinct agreement on the part of members of the committee that its objective is eminently desirable, that there is opportunity for very valuable public service in its work, and that while not as much has been achieved as members would naturally wish, there has been a measure of real accomplishment by the committee in its work thus far.
The leader of the opposition (Mr. Hanson) asked-and I think a similar request was made by the leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation party (Mr. Coldwell)- that I should state distinctly the view of the government with respect to the scope of the committee and give the house an assurance that there would be no restriction on its work by seeking to narrow down the extent of the committee's authority as set forth in the resolution. I wish to give that assurance emphatically and unequivocally. The desire of the government in establishing this committee is to have it investigate as fully and as completely as it possibly can matters which its members or others may bring to the committee as proper subjects for investigation. No group of members of the house could feel more deeply concerned about the expenditure of vast sums of money than the government itself does, and we look upon this committee not as a body that is investigating the government but as a body that is assisting the government in its control of public expenditures. I should like that view to be fully appreciated by all hon. members on the committee. Indeed, nothing has been more satisfactory, I think, to those of us who have this responsibility to carry than to observe that the members of the committee themselves have felt that the opportunities they have on the committee lie so largely in that direction. It is encouraging to know that they have felt that they do not regard themselves as a committee searching for

War Expenditures-Mr. Mackenzie King
scandal but rather as a body of members of this house who are seeking to render a public service in the matter of seeing that all possible economies are effected in connection with war expenditures and that matters which should be still further investigated may be brought to the attention of the government or of some committee of this house for that purpose.
In that regard I should like to draw the attention of the house to the significance of one statement in particular which was made this afternoon by the Minister of National War Services. Let me preface my remarks on that by saying that many have criticized the fact that the proceedings of the committee are in camera. But as my hon. friend the minister said, the purpose of sitting in camera is not that of seeking to conceal information. It is really a method of procuring information which could not be possible if the committee's proceedings were in public. That point, I think, has not been sufficiently dwelt upon. The very fact that the committee is sitting in camera and can bring before it any of the officials of any department connected with the war effort and can examine fully and in detail all matters that come before it, enables the members of the committee to obtain much more information than would otherwise be possible.
May I supplement that by drawing attention to what has been said so often in the British house, which is that while the public is not being informed daily of the proceedings of the committee, hon. members of that committee gain information and knowledge to a degree that would not be possible in any other way. If, in acquiring knowledge with respect to government contracts and matters of one kind or another, they feel there is need for fuller inquiry, there is nothing to prevent them from bringing up on the floor of the house questions which they think ought to be investigated further and asking for information from the ministry or seeking to obtain further inquiries before the committee of public accounts, if they wish so to do.
Viewed in that light I think it will be seen that there is an opportunity much greater than appears on the surface in the work of the committee. The members of the committee at Westminster have come across matters which they thought would not bear the light of day. They did not wish to expose them to the public gaze in a sensational way by having the proceedings carried on in public; they have felt that by having these matters appear in the press it would-I will not say be of assistance to the enemy, but be
a comfort to the enemy, who delights in anything which will tend to create discord and suspicion in a country to which he is opposed. The opportunity, however, has thereby been afforded members of the committee to go to the minister of the department concerned and bring to his attention matters which they thought ought to be discussed.
Let me say on behalf of my colleagues and myself that if the members of this committee in the course of their investigations have reason to believe that there is some transaction that is not creditable or if there are good grounds of suspicion that there is some dealing that is not honourable, I invite them to bring these matters immediately to the attention of the minister who is at the head of the department; and if the minister does not find means to have the matter satisfactorily dealt with, then I would suggest that a direct request be made of the government to have the matter investigated by the committee on public accounts.
The reason why the war expenditures committee is not being regarded as a committee on public accounts is that we already have a committee on public accounts, a standing committee of this house, to deal with matters that should be dealt with in relation to public accounts. As I have indicated, the function of the war expenditure committee is not that of a committee on public accounts. Its duty is to investigate with a view to protecting the government's war effort in as many ways as may be possible, particularly in relation to unwise expenditures and unwise methods in regard to these expenditures.
The question of publicity has been fully explained by my colleague, and the question of the extent of the powers of the committee I think I have dealt with in a way to confirm the views already expressed by the minister in that regard.
Something has been said about the length of time which has been taken in setting up the committee, the insufficient time which the committee has had for looking into expenditures, and the lateness of the session at which the committee is now being constituted. I would be the last to deny that there has been ground for fair comment and criticism in that direction, but I would ask hon. members, when they speak about the committee not having been established at the very first session, to recall the matters to which the government had to give immediate attention. It seems to me that we would have been inviting unnecessary suspicion with regard to our own departments and administrators if, before we had begun to incur expenditures to any considerable extent, we had undertaken to form the

committee, with other committees we already had in existence, at a much earlier time than we did.
Moreover, as hon. members themselves have found out, in the work of the committee the matters to be inquired into are so vast and extensive, the numbers of contracts so great, the whole business so large, that unless the methods of the committee were properly organized at the outset, unless the committee got a bird's-eye view, so to speak, of the whole field to be surveyed and a dhe appreciation of its own functions in the clearest possible way before entering on examination in detail, the time of the committee would have been very largely wasted and very little in the way of effective action would have followed.
I think hon. members who are on the committee will agree that, under the direction of the chairman, who was then a private member of the house, an excellent foundation was laid for the further work of the committee, and that much of the time that was taken up in organization will begin from now on to bear fruit in abundance.
The hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Douglas) and others have spoken of the desirability of enlisting as largely as possible the services of the various members in connection with work on committees. I can assure him and other hon. members that the government is only too anxious to have the members' time employed as actively and efficiently as possible. There are now-it may surprise hon. members to hear me say it-no less than twenty-two committees; there will be, when the defence of Canada regulations committee is appointed, twenty-three committees at work this session. There are seven select committees, and the fifteen standing committees. That is a considerable number; indeed, some complaint has been made to-day that so many committees are meeting it is difficult to have members attend to the extent that they should.
Possibly there is room for improvement in the arrangement of the meetings of the different committees, and, speaking for myself, I should be wholly favourable to having the committee on war expenditures enlarged if that is going to help to further the work for which the committee was intended. I shall be glad to take up that matter with my colleagues; I think they will view it sympathetically; and if the committee itself, after a meeting, feels that its work could be better performed by having its membership enlarged to some extent, I for one shall be prepared to do what I can to have that recommendation favourably received by the house.
I might say the same in respect to other recommendations that may come from the

committee to the house. I believe, now that the work is generally recognized to be of the importance that it is, this house will be ready to approve almost any recommendation which comes to it from the committee itself.
I do not know that there is more I should add at the moment; indeed, I do not want to have this debate go over to to-morrow. I would, however, not like to conclude without expressing appreciation to members of the house, and particularly to the members of the committee, of the general acceptance of the resolution which is now before the house, and which I believe will pass unanimously to-night.

Will the Prime Minister state whether it will be possible at this session for private members to attend the sessions of the committee, not to take part in them, but to attend? It was allowed at some sessions which were held last year.

speechtext: I believe that is a privilege of private members at all times. I feel certain, if the committee themselves wish to have that liberty granted, it will be granted in a moment. I can see no reason why private members should not be permitted to attend at. any time.
